operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory fee-cap compression or administrative hold
platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules
platform_risks.impact: Reduced net fee margin or extended cash conversion cycle
platform_risks.detection_metric: County/state rejection notice rate and days-to-payout variance
platform_risks.fallback: Diversify across multi-state dockets and use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required

operator_plays.name: SAM.gov / Municipal RFP Scraping & Prime-Subcontractor Spread Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Scrape federal SAM.gov, state procurement portals, and municipal bid boards for low-bid-density service solicitations (janitorial, grounds, courier, translation, IT staffing), pairing compliant proposal automation with vetted local fulfillment subcontractors for a 15–30% management spread.
inputs: SAM.gov Contract Opportunities API & state/municipal e-procurement feeds
Historical FPDS award pricing benchmark database
Vetted local subcontractor network with FAR limitation-on-subcontracting compliance
workflow: Screen daily federal, state, and municipal RFPs/RFQs with <3 historical bidders and clear unit-price schedules
Benchmark winning historical unit rates via FPDS/FOIA award records and lock in binding back-to-back quotes from insured local operators
Submit compliant bid packages and manage billing, insurance, and QA reporting while retaining a 15–30% prime-management or authorized broker spread
metrics: Bid-to-award win rate (%) on low-competition solicitations

platform_risks.failure_mode: FAR 52.219-14 (Limitations on Subcontracting) violation or illegal pass-through scheme
platform_risks.trigger: Bidding small-business set-aside contracts and subcontracting 100% of the work to non-similarly-situated entities without performing required prime share
platform_risks.impact: Contract termination for default, False Claims Act liability, or SAM.gov debarment
platform_risks.detection_metric: Subcontracted labor-cost percentage strictly within FAR 52.219-14 limits (<=50% for services unless partnering with similarly situated small businesses)
platform_risks.fallback: Bid unrestricted commercial/municipal contracts without set-aside caps, or team exclusively with 'similarly situated entities' under 13 CFR § 125.6

operator_plays.name: Multi-Account Presale Code & Limited-Mintage Allocation Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Operating hundreds of aged, human-scored 'free' fan-club, ticketing (Ticketmaster Verified Fan / AXS), U.S. Mint, and limited-edition luxury/collectible accounts—each backed by unique residential proxies, aged browser profiles, and virtual card numbers (VCCs)—to multiply lottery/queue odds by 100x–500x on strict 'limit 1–4 per account' releases trading at instant 50–300% secondary-market premiums.
inputs: Aged ticketing, fan-club, and sovereign-mint account fleet with clean purchase histories
Anti-detect browser matrix with residential ISP proxies and unique SIM/SMS verification lines
Corporate virtual credit card (VCC) issuance API (Extend/Ramp/Slash) with distinct billing descriptors
workflow: Monitor upcoming concert tours, playoff games, U.S. Mint numismatic releases, and limited collectible drops with secondary-market spreads >=50%
Register the aged account fleet across presale lotteries and waiting rooms to secure high-priority access codes and low queue positions
Execute checkouts strictly on high-margin allocations (front-row/pit seats, low-mintage proof coins) using isolated VCCs per household profile
Flip allocations immediately via direct consignment, verified ticket exchanges (StubHub/SeatGeek/Vivid API), or pre-committed wholesale buyers
metrics: Presale code / top-1,000 queue-position hit rate (%) across the account cluster
Net realized secondary-market spread (%) after exchange/consignment fees
Inventory hold time (hours/days from checkout to settled resale payout)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Order cancellation or queue-score penalty from device/payment fingerprint linkage
platform_risks.trigger: Reusing identical billing addresses, card BINs, or browser WebGL/Canvas fingerprints across Household-Limit-restricted drops
platform_risks.impact: Canceled orders, revoked presale codes, or permanent account flagging
platform_risks.detection_metric: Post-checkout order survival rate (%) and queue-score tier telemetry
platform_risks.fallback: Maintain genuine distributed buyer consortiums with unique residential addresses, distinct bank BINs, and pre-sold wholesale buyer commitments before checkout

operator_plays.name: Section 321 "De Minimis" & Border Bonded-Warehouse Tariff Split-Shipping Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Routing bulk sea/air container imports for high-tariff DTC and marketplace brands into Tijuana (IMMEX) or Canadian border-zone bonded 3PL warehouses instead of US ports, then fulfilling individual US consumer orders across the border daily under 19 U.S.C. § 1321 (Section 321 Entry Type 86)—legally eliminating 15%–42.5% customs duties on qualifying consumer parcels and charging brands 35–50% of the saved tariff bill plus 3PL fulfillment fees.
inputs: USITC Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) database cross-referenced against US Customs Bill-of-Lading import records (ImportYeti / Panjiva / Datamyne)
Nearshore Mexican IMMEX or Canadian customs-bonded fulfillment center 5–15 miles from San Ysidro/Otay Mesa or Windsor/Blaine border crossings
Automated CBP ACE Entry Type 86 manifest software transmitting 10-digit HTS and consignee data per individual consumer parcel
workflow: Scrape public maritime Bill-of-Lading records to identify US apparel, footwear, luggage, and consumer-goods brands importing 20+ containers/yr in 18%–37.5% HTS duty brackets
Divert the client's ocean containers in-bond (IT/T&E bond) directly to the nearshore border-zone fulfillment facility without paying US bulk entry duties
Sync the warehouse WMS with the brand's Shopify/Amazon store so each US consumer order (<$800 retail value, 1 per person per day) is picked, packed, and cleared via CBP Entry Type 86 at $0 duty
Line-item bill the brand for standard pick-and-pack fulfillment plus a 35–50% contingency split of the verified customs duties eliminated
metrics: Annualized customs duty eliminated ($500k–$10M+/yr per enterprise brand client)
Net tariff-savings share + 3PL margin ($) per parcel cleared across the border
CBP Type 86 automated release rate (>99.4%) and border transit time (<6 hours to USPS/FedEx domestic injection)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory exclusion of specific Section 301 country-of-origin SKUs from Section 321 de minimis eligibility
platform_risks.trigger: Executive/statutory rulemaking removing China-origin Section 301 HTS codes from Entry Type 86 eligibility or tightening 10-digit HTS description rules
platform_risks.impact: Loss of Section 321 duty exemption on affected country-of-origin SKUs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Real-time HTS + Country-of-Origin eligibility screen in the WMS before container booking
platform_risks.fallback: Focus on non-301 origin goods (Vietnam, India, EU, Bangladesh, Cambodia) where high MFN duties (16%–32% on apparel/footwear/textiles) remain 100% Section 321 exempt, and pair with CBP First-Sale Valuation for remaining SKUs

operator_plays.name: Authorized-Distributor "Diversion" & Grey-Market Luxury / Medical Consumables Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Exploiting multinational manufacturers' 35–60% regional price discrimination by using foreign corporate purchasing entities to buy container-loads of 100% authentic branded goods (luxury fragrances, prestige cosmetics, Swiss watches, OTC diabetic test strips, salon haircare, OEM imaging supplies) from over-quota authorized distributors in emerging/EMEA/LATAM markets and importing them into US off-price retail (TJX, Costco, Burlington) and Amazon wholesale channels under the Supreme Court's First-Sale Doctrine (*Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons*).
inputs: Global wholesale price-book matrix comparing US net distributor pricing against EMEA, LATAM, Eastern European, and Asian-Pacific tier-1 distributor net pricing
Foreign purchasing subsidiaries (UAE, Poland, Panama, Singapore, Cyprus) with clean trade references and escrow inspection facilities
SGS/Bureau Veritas pre-shipment authenticity verification and batch-code sanitization SOPs
workflow: Identify authentic global SKUs with >40% wholesale price spreads between emerging-market distributor books and US off-price wholesale demand
Approach regional authorized distributors near end-of-quarter who need to move $500k–$5M in excess allocation to hit their manufacturer volume-tier rebate
Purchase the sealed master cases via a foreign trading entity, conduct third-party SGS lot authentication, and remove secondary distributor tracking labels that could identify the source distributor
Import the goods legally under First-Sale exhaustion and flip on back-to-back POs to US off-price retail chains, pharmacy wholesalers, and verified marketplace aggregators
metrics: Gross landed price spread (22–45% net margin) between foreign distributor cost and US wholesale PO price
Inventory cash-conversion cycle (days from escrow release to US buyer wire settlement)
100% lot-level manufacturer authenticity verification and chain-of-custody pass rate

platform_risks.failure_mode: Brand-owner Lanham Act 'material difference' trademark challenge or marketplace invoice rejection
platform_risks.trigger: Importing foreign-language packaging or altered warranty/formulation SKUs that differ materially from the US domestic version
platform_risks.impact: CBP detention or Amazon brand-gating suppression on specific ASINs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Pre-purchase SKU inspection confirming identical UPC/EAN, multi-language compliant labeling, and identical physical formulation
platform_risks.fallback: Trade strictly in globally identical universal-packaging SKUs (duty-free prestige fragrances, universal OEM consumables) and sell primarily via direct B2B purchase orders to off-price retail chains and regional wholesalers rather than single-account Amazon storefronts

operator_plays.name: Certificate-of-Need (CON) & Decommissioned Hospital Imaging-Suite Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Acquire or option decommissioned imaging assets where approved site capacity has value, separating equipment resale economics from nontransferable or change-of-control-sensitive CON authority.
inputs: State CON decisions and hospital closure notices
Equipment service logs and site engineering surveys
Regulatory transfer guidance and buyer commitments
workflow: 1. Identify closing imaging suites and inventory equipment, permits, and lease rights
2. Confirm CON status, transfer restrictions, radiation licensing, and deinstallation costs
3. Negotiate approval-contingent asset purchases with qualified operators and equipment buyers
4. Close after regulatory clearance and document certified removal, installation, and acceptance

platform_risks.failure_mode: CON authority lapses or cannot transfer
platform_risks.trigger: Closure, relocation, or ownership change outside approved conditions
platform_risks.impact: Loss of site premium and stranded equipment carrying costs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Outstanding regulatory conditions and days to permit expiry
platform_risks.fallback: Exit under approval contingencies or sell inspected equipment separately without representing transferable operating authority

chapters.question_prompt: Where do government surplus auctions actually happen, and how do I register, search, and place bids on the main platforms?
chapters.title: Finding the Sales: Government Auction Platforms and How Bidding Works
chapters.subtitle: GSAAuctions.gov online and offline bidding, GovDeals listings, Public Surplus, RealEstateSales.gov registration, UX Auctions search tools, and city, county, state, and federal sale sources
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the inventory is real, public, and fragmented: East Coast Classics found Delaware, New Castle County, and Wilmington each selling through a different platform, while UX Auctions and GovAuctions name GSA Auctions, GovDeals, Public Surplus, and Municibid as the core channels, no dealer license required. The street math is fee-driven: GovDeals buyer's premiums run 5% to 12.5%, US Gov Bid charges a $100 one-time registration plus a $60 wire fee, and Public Surplus caps card purchases at $4,000. UX Auctions logged 310 Florida running vehicles under $3,000 and Norfolk keyed vehicles at a $1,300 middle price versus $550 without keys. Winning hinges on proxy bids, soft-close extensions, reserves, and short pickup windows. The split is over condition risk: Greg Berry sells $70-battery upside on non-runners, while East Coast Classics passed on Crown Vics too rough to export.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every practitioner agrees on is that the sales are real and open to anyone. GovAuctions frames it bluntly: agencies are legally required to dispose of seized and surplus property, cannot hold it indefinitely, and push it to the public through auctions, with most lots needing no special license or dealer credentials [x8_btciMVuY @ 00:00:15]. UX Auctions sets the bar at two conditions: if you are old enough to sign a contract and you can pay, you can bid, no dealer license and no connections required [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:02:42]. Greg Berry, who founded Municibid in 2006 after watching a town council sell a police car worth $3,000 for $300 or $400 to one or two interested people, says anyone in the United States and Canada can bid, and roughly 80 percent of the bidder base is businesses: landscapers buying dump trucks, snow removal outfits buying plow trucks, construction firms buying heavy equipment [pRzKRg71z4s @ 00:09:43]. The supply is also not a trickle. Matthew Lesko pegs GSA Auctions alone at $250 million a year in vehicles, furniture, electronics, and machinery, with roughly 300 sales running at any time and an estimated one and a half to two billion dollars in federal property moving annually [Ezeprg6O_GU @ 00:00:02].

The second consensus point is that no single site holds the market, so finding sales is legwork. East Coast Classics calls the search the hardest part of the whole process, says Google is your best friend for queries like public auctions or public surplus in your area, and reports that in Delaware the state sells through US Gov Bid, New Castle County through GovDeals, and the city of Wilmington through Public Surplus, all within minutes of each other [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:01:38]. MrDavidAdelman makes the same complaint: there is no consolidated place listing everything, local, state, and federal governments tend not to cooperate, and listings may only mention some of the items being sold, so call the local or state office, check the newspaper, and look at notices posted in city and county buildings [gnsqwRYhRPY @ 00:01:51]. UX Auctions maps the channels: cities and counties on GovDeals, Public Surplus, and Municibid, the federal fleet through GSA Auctions and GSA Fleet sales, some agencies through hired local auction companies, and impounded cars straight off city tow lots, with a sale sometimes listed only a week or two [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:04:23]. GovAuctions adds that the biggest challenge across three platforms is simply not missing lots [ubzNe62V_y4 @ 00:01:21].

Every speaker who touches condition lands on the same rule: government property sells as is, and the bidder carries the risk. UX Auctions points to fine print on a real Florida listing stating the description rests on a limited 5 to 10 minute visual inspection, then reminds buyers there is no warranty and no returns, so zoom in on tires, dash, body, and engine bay or go see it [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:08:55]. Greg Berry tells Municibid buyers to be buyer beware, ask every question, and use the on-site viewing most selling agencies allow to kick the tires before bidding, adding that pretty much everything on Municibid sells as is and largely out of warranty [pRzKRg71z4s @ 00:15:01]. East Coast Classics is the harshest on this point: get off your rump, make the phone call, schedule an appointment, and physically inspect, because one car that read and photographed well online could be smelled before reaching the windows and turned out to be a former K9 unit [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:05:55]. GovAuctions closes the loop for resellers: condition is often unknown, there are no returns, and shipping can eat into your margin fast, so know what you are looking at before you bid [x8_btciMVuY @ 00:01:05].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The fee stack changes by platform, and East Coast Classics has run the numbers on all three Delaware channels. US Gov Bid now charges a one-time $100 registration fee but carries no buyer's premium, which makes it cheapest on higher-dollar buys; the catch is payment, either a wire with a $60 processing fee that recently rose from $30, plus roughly $30 your own bank charges, or an overnighted cashier's check, so a $10 pair of jack stands can land near $100 all-in, while a $3,200 Chevy Tahoe came in at a little under 3 percent in fees [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:03:09]. GovDeals registration costs nothing, but a buyer's premium set by each municipality runs from 5 percent to 12.5 percent, offset by easy PayPal or credit card payment and customer service seven days a week [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:04:12]. Public Surplus files vehicles under motor pools, places a hold on your card for a portion of the bid once bidding passes $500, and caps credit card purchases at $4,000 [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:05:25]. UX Auctions tells new bidders to check four terms before anything else: payment method and deadline, buyer's premium, pickup window, and whether you get a title or a bill of sale [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:06:20].

The bidding engine runs on proxy logic. GSA explains that an English-style online auction accepts a flat bid, which is the starting bid or current bid plus the increment, or a proxy bid set at the most you will pay; the system spends only enough to beat a competing proxy plus one increment, the greater proxy always wins, an exact tie goes to whoever entered first, and an inactivity period at the end means the sale closes only after a set stretch with no bids [JzuRczRAlW8 @ 00:02:23]. UX Auctions tells bidders to enter their number as the max and let the system work, because early prices mean almost nothing: the Monday before a Florida sale, 103 Explorers sat at $5 to $10, and Guilford County lots were stuck at $200 to $250 days before close; many sites also add minutes when a late bid lands, so sniping the last second is unreliable, and reserve lots do not sell if bidding stays under the seller's floor [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:15:10]. GSA's redesign flags lots yellow at one to two hours left and red under one hour, and lists the top four high bids under the place-bid button [csOCrIHnuSo @ 00:01:47].

Pricing your number comes from sold data, not dealer stickers. UX Auctions says to pull the middle price of the same year and model, ideally in the same state over recent months, then adjust down for high miles, no key, or a branded title, and add bid, buyer's premium, fees, towing or shipping, title and registration, and inspection-day repairs to get the real cost; the keys gap alone is stark, with Norfolk keyed vehicles at a $1,300 middle price against $550 without [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:08:33]. The UX Network's November 19, 2026 report gives fresh comps: a 2009 Crown Victoria with 106,000 miles at $2,405, a 2019 Tahoe at $6,651, a 2011 International tandem dump truck at $5,200, and a 1987 Humvee diesel with 3,500 miles at $7,506 [c9mCACUk14Y @ 00:01:26]. East Coast Classics watched Crown Vics live: a 2003 captain's car with 108,000 miles stalled at $450, a 153,000-mile unit with 4,700 idle hours drew six bidders to $625 with hours to go, and a clean 118,000-mile county car sold for $650 to a single bidder [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:11:03]. GovAuctions puts the clock at 3 to 10 day auctions, 5 to 15 business days to pay, and 1 to 4 week pickups [Ie7zxVOXjeE @ 00:01:21].

callout.title: Edges the Regulars Use
callout.body: Small habits that separate repeat buyers from first-timers chasing listing photos.
items: Search US Gov Bid past auctions going back years to pull historical selling prices on everything sold before you set a max [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:03:24].

Work the yard: a maintenance supervisor who openly shared what they knew about the fleet turned one county lot into a potential honey hole, with every car there slated for upcoming auctions [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:11:03].

Read the seller playbook: GovDeals tells agencies to run 7 to 10 days, end Monday through Thursday in the afternoon or evening, avoid weekends and holidays, and stagger end times at least 10 minutes apart, so watch those closing windows [GovDeals Media — Q4B13yVVzZQ @ 00:01:11].

Cannot make inspection day? Hire a mobile inspection service with ASE certified mechanics to check the vehicle and send a photo report before you bid, provided the yard allows outside inspectors [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:10:18].

sop_steps.title: Map Every Local Seller
sop_steps.action: Search for the state, county, and city auction platforms in your area and register on each.
sop_steps.detail: Google public auctions or public surplus for your area and expect each level of government to use a different company, then register as a bidder on each [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:01:25]. Hunt the agency that would logically own the item, such as an agriculture agency for used tractors [MrDavidAdelman — gnsqwRYhRPY @ 00:03:09].

sop_steps.title: Register and Read the Terms
sop_steps.action: Create accounts, keep a card on file where required, and read the four terms on every sale.
sop_steps.detail: Signup is free on most sites with name, address, phone, and email, some require a credit card on file, and the terms to check are payment method and deadline, buyer's premium, pickup window, and title or bill of sale [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:06:01]. For federal real estate, verify through Login.gov, submit the bid form and registration deposit, and register separately for each property [GSA (General Services Administration) — zFGATosXViU @ 00:04:11].

sop_steps.title: Inspect and Set Your Number
sop_steps.action: Go on inspection day with tools, then price off sold middle prices plus every added cost.
sop_steps.detail: Bring a flashlight, rag, gloves, phone, and an OBD2 scanner if allowed, and walk away from frame rust you can poke through, signs of a flood, or a VIN that does not match; everything else gets factored into the bid [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:11:50].

sop_steps.title: Bid Proxy, Pay Fast, Remove Legally
sop_steps.action: Enter your max as a proxy, pay inside the deadline, and have removal sorted before close.
sop_steps.detail: Set a firm maximum, expect payment deadlines as tight as two to three business days, and bring valid ID plus proof of payment at pickup [The Salmon Runs — jaeWKn_Nu68 @ 00:01:08]. Know how the vehicle leaves the lot: in Delaware a $20 temporary tag gives 60 days of legal driving, while other sellers require a tow [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:06:23].

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is over where to hunt. East Coast Classics treats discovery as a manual grind: Google public auctions or public surplus for your area and keep digging, because in Delaware the state sells through US Gov Bid, New Castle County through GovDeals, and the city of Wilmington through Public Surplus [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:01:25]. The channel calls GovDeals the big dog with robust filtering that can still overwhelm an unfocused buyer, ranks US Gov Bid as a small player, and slots Public Surplus in the middle. UX Auctions runs the opposite playbook: one search box at uxsearch.app that hits GovDeals, GSA, Public Surplus, Municibid and police auction sites at once, plus a schedule page that maps every police and government sale it finds [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:00:20]. GovAuctions splits the difference, framing GovDeals as the high-volume classroom for learning how prices settle and Public Surplus as the place sleeper deals from schools and counties hide, then telling buyers to work a fixed schedule with a short list of categories and locations rather than checking every site by hand [ubzNe62V_y4 @ 00:01:05]. MrDavidAdelman goes fully analog: no consolidated list exists, so call or email local and state offices, read the local paper, and scan postings at city and county buildings [gnsqwRYhRPY @ 00:02:23].

Cost structure is where the platforms diverge hardest, and East Coast Classics has run the numbers on all three. US Gov Bid now charges a one-time $100 registration fee but no buyer's premium, which makes it the lowest-fee venue on higher-dollar buys; their $3,200 Chevy Tahoe landed at a little less than 3% in fees [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:03:24]. The catch is payment: wire the money with a $60 processing fee, up from $30, plus roughly $30 from your own bank, or overnight a cashier's check, so a $10 pair of jack stands turns into a $100 purchase. GovDeals flips that model with free registration, PayPal or credit card payment, and a buyer's premium they have seen run from 5% to 12.5% depending on the municipality. Public Surplus places a hold on your card once bidding passes $500 and caps card purchases at $4,000. UX Auctions confirms the patchwork, warning that some sales take credit cards while others accept only a cashier's check or wire, and that the buyer's premium sits on top of the winning bid [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:06:37]. The payment clock itself is disputed: The Salmon Runs says deadlines typically land within two to three business days [jaeWKn_Nu68 @ 00:01:08], while GovAuctions quotes five to fifteen business days [Ie7zxVOXjeE @ 00:01:21].

Not everyone bids in a timed online lot. Matthew Lesko pitches the free route: Lesko says small businesses, including veteran-owned ones, plus nonprofits, schools, clinics, child care centers and museums can get surplus for free, citing a requirement of at least 51% ownership or control by economically disadvantaged citizens and income under $400,000, and recalling a nonprofit radio station that landed an ex Air Force base [Ezeprg6O_GU @ 00:03:16]. GSA runs a parallel offline lane: sealed bids by mail or email stay sealed until the date on the invitation for bid, term contracts can demand recurring removals over a set period, and fixed-price retail sales go first-come, first-served [Dga3YkAiGmw @ 00:01:04]. Greg Berry of Municibid describes the resale playbook instead: buyers turning fire hoses into wallets sold on Etsy, a car guy who accidentally bought 20 or 30 traffic lights and built a side business reselling them, refinishers flipping wood furniture, and bulk lots bought at a discount then sold off individually [pRzKRg71z4s @ 00:10:19]. GovAuctions frames the format choice as temperament: online timed auctions run over several days and let you research at your own pace, while live events move faster with real-time bidding [Ie7zxVOXjeE @ 00:00:48].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Condition is where buyers bleed. East Coast Classics went to Avalon, New Jersey to vet Crown Victorias for a buddy named Frank: the 2003 captain's car at 108,000 miles carried a long door scratch and fender rust, the Oreo car had rust, sticker shadows and 4,700 idle hours, and two more on a second lot would not start, one needing a fuel pump and one a starter, leaving them parts cars bid in the high $300s [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:09:22]. Another car read good and looked good online, yet East Coast Classics smelled it before reaching the windows and later learned it was a former K9 car. UX Auctions points out that listing descriptions can rest on a limited 5 to 10 minute visual inspection and that government vehicles sell as is with no warranty and no returns [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:09:14]. Its walk-away list is frame rust you can poke through, flood signs like a musty smell, damp carpet or a water line, and a VIN that does not match the listing. Keys move price too: in Norfolk, keyed vehicles sold at a middle price of $1,300 versus $550 without [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:08:33]. Greg Berry's counterpoint is that a non-runner may only need a $70 battery [pRzKRg71z4s @ 00:15:50].

The second trap is logistics after the hammer. East Coast Classics has seen removal windows of seven days at some lots and two at others, and notes Delaware sells a $20 temporary tag good for 60 days while other jurisdictions force a tow [q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:06:23]. UX Auctions documents the penalties: miss a payment deadline and you can lose the vehicle and get blocked from bidding again; Guilford County gave a three-day pickup window, Wednesday through Friday with no other times, and Montgomery County, Maryland charges a daily storage fee before forfeiting the vehicle with no refund [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:17:24]. Montgomery County also requires a tow truck, tow dolly, trailer, temporary plates or dealer plates to move it, and its buyers must apply for a salvage title within 90 days, while Norfolk buyers get a bill of sale and affidavit with 30 days to file at the Virginia DMV. GovAuctions warns that condition is often unknown, there are no returns, and shipping can eat into your margin fast [x8_btciMVuY @ 00:01:23]. MrDavidAdelman watched a pallet of computers go for less than the cost of a single computer while in the right place at the right time, but without a truck [gnsqwRYhRPY @ 00:05:28].

The last check is the bidder's own head. UX Auctions calls getting caught up in the moment the biggest mistake new bidders make, and prescribes the fix: price off real winning bids for the same year, model and state, use the middle price rather than an average one crazy sale can distort, then total bid plus buyer's premium, fees, towing or shipping, title, registration and repairs [Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:12:10]. Early prices are noise; on the Monday before the Florida sale, 103 Explorers still sat at $5 to $10, sites extend the clock when late bids land, and a reserve can kill the sale even if you are high bidder. The Salmon Runs adds sales tax to that cost stack and says to set a firm maximum and stick to it [jaeWKn_Nu68 @ 00:00:52]. Chill Crayon Explains frames these as competitive auctions rather than bargains handed out, where the real trick is calculating every cost before placing a bid [J0zoheNKu-E @ 00:03:55]. MrDavidAdelman confirms $100 cars exist but warns they will most likely not be in mint condition, so kick the tires, test drive if allowed, and check the car is not a salvage car [gnsqwRYhRPY @ 00:03:30].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Place a Bid
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, forfeiture or bad buy the practitioners reported. If any one fails, pass on the lot and wait for the next sale.
items: Read the terms of sale for payment method and deadline, buyer's premium, pickup window, and whether you get a title or a bill of sale, because this is where people get burned [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:06:20].
Walk away from frame rust you can poke through, any flood sign such as a musty smell, damp carpet or water line, or a VIN that does not match the listing [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:11:50].
Confirm the removal window, which ran from seven days down to two, and how the vehicle legally leaves the lot, temporary tag or tow, before bidding [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:06:23].
Price in sales tax, buyer's premiums and shipping fees, then set a firm maximum bid that fits the budget and stick to it [The Salmon Runs — jaeWKn_Nu68 @ 00:00:52].

chapters.pull_quote: "Take your number, write it down and stick to it. If the bidding goes past it, let it go. There's another sale next week." — UX Auctions (Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:13:51).
action_checklist: Search public auctions and public surplus separately for your city, county and state, since each may sell through a different platform such as US Gov Bid, GovDeals or Public Surplus [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:01:25].
Register as a bidder on each platform you find, budgeting the $100 one-time US Gov Bid fee and expecting free registration on GovDeals [East Coast Classics — q09PUtJPIxs @ 00:02:09].
Pull real winning bids for the same year, model and state from recent months and use the middle price, not the highest or lowest [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:13:14].

Inspect in person with a flashlight, rag, gloves, phone and an OBD2 scanner, or hire a mobile ASE-certified inspection service if the yard allows outside inspectors [UX Auctions — Z87d62pWVEk @ 00:10:36].
Enter a proxy bid at the maximum you are willing to pay so GSA Auctions bids on your behalf only as much as needed to lead [GSA (General Services Administration) — JzuRczRAlW8 @ 00:02:03].
After winning, confirm payment processed, bring valid ID and proof of payment to pickup, and inspect the item on site against its description [The Salmon Runs — jaeWKn_Nu68 @ 00:01:41].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find, inspect, and win government-surplus cars, trucks, and police vehicles at a price that leaves room for profit?
chapters.title: Buying Fleet Cars, Trucks, and Police Vehicles
chapters.subtitle: State and local vehicle sales, seized-vehicle lanes, GSA online truck buys, on-site F-250 inspections, sub-$5,000 rental-fleet picks, GovDeals tips for new accounts, and splitting a $900 Expedition for profit
chapters.executive_summary: Operators buying retired fleet cars, trucks, and police units agree the vehicles come serviced but sold as-is: good tires and oil changes, no records, no test drives, and wrecks rarely repaired. Street mechanics center on GovDeals radius searches, GSA registration through the auction house, OBD scans and door-sticker checks at preview, a $12 to $15 VIN history, and buyer premiums running about 5% on GSA up to 15% at sheriff sales. Reported numbers range from a $900 Expedition landing near $2,000 all-in against a $5,000-plus KBB to an F-250 hammering at $4,150 and closing at $4,669 with fees. Practitioners split on sniping, with Top 5 Autos pushing last-minute bids while Street Rat Garage says extensions kill the tactic, and on whether real bargains exist at all, since East Coast Classics calls them few and far between.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across lots in Indiana, Texas, Delaware, and Arizona, the operators converge on one baseline: retired fleet units are maintained but unvetted. Street Rat Garage reports that fleet units arrive with good tires and regular oil changes, while wrecks are rarely repaired [qieQr_fEJQ8 @ 00:16:16]. AJ at Handyman Process says GSA is pretty thorough about maintaining its vehicles, but you do not get those records, so bring a mechanic [FZRiWN_dcS4 @ 00:06:55]. East Coast Classics, who has bought a couple dozen cars at surplus sales, confirms service history is limited and warns that genuine deals are few and far between [g9Wt5wG1aGM @ 00:01:08]. The paint is usually gray or white, the drivetrain usually saw scheduled service, and the unknowns sit in damage the agency never fixed. Street Rat Garage adds a reading rule for listings: state employees write up every tiny leak, so a scary condition report should be taken with a grain of salt rather than treated as a death sentence [cqTAqIJLC10 @ 00:15:09]. AJ also calls selection hit or miss, so the consensus play is patience: walk every sale, log what each unit actually brings, and only pounce when a clean fleet truck slips under the crowd.

The second point of agreement is that you buy blind on the drive cycle. East Coast Classics lays out the preview rules: start the car, feel the brakes, engage the transmission, test HVAC, lights, and electrical, and plug in an OBD code reader, but the biggest restriction is you cannot drive the car, and some auctions allow no on-site inspection at all [g9Wt5wG1aGM @ 00:03:20]. Street Rat Garage gets the same terms on GovDeals: call ahead, start it, roll it forward and back, but no test drive and no shop inspection [cqTAqIJLC10 @ 00:08:33]. At the San Antonio dealer auction, AJ finds most if not all units unlocked with keys inside, so the move is to fire it up and hook an OBD reader during the preview day [FZRiWN_dcS4 @ 00:01:50]. Because the price must absorb that risk, Tool Demos argues these buys only make sense if you have mechanical skill and patience; their $900 ex-fire-rescue Expedition was cheap precisely because of an audible engine noise, which turned out to be a scored cylinder-three exhaust cam lobe and a destroyed roller follower [EFXJtp6q_B8 @ 00:01:31]. The operators agree that the discount exists because the government will not let you find the problem first, and the buyer who can diagnose by ear and scanner collects that spread.

Every operator who posted receipts treats the hammer price as a partial number. Top 5 Autos pegs the buyer premium at roughly 5% on GSA Auctions, up to 10% on GovPlanet, and up to 15% at sheriff sales [WFVGJDWST7I @ 00:05:16]. UX Auctions documented a 2006 Southport fire department F-250 with 157,119 miles hammer at $4,150 after 47 bids and land at $4,669 with fees [IUAs4NGQfyo @ 00:05:15]. Junk Solutions Experts LLC won a school-district F-150 at $2,000 and was in for $2,250 after buyer premium and tax, noting that can take a little bit out of your profit [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:13:42]. The crowd is the other cost: Tool Demos warns you can definitely get into bidding wars with people, and that is how the price gets out of control [EFXJtp6q_B8 @ 00:09:31]. Tool Demos landed the Expedition at roughly $2,000 cash in against a KBB of $5,000 to $5,500 after holding the buy under $1,000. The working consensus is to fix a ceiling from comps before the sale opens, price in premium, tax, and transport, and walk away the moment the clock or the room pushes past it.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Sourcing starts with geography. Street Rat Garage runs GovDeals Advanced Search, sets Locations to a radius around a ZIP, 150 miles from 46201 in their case, and then opens a seller's other items to see that agency's full inventory [cqTAqIJLC10 @ 00:04:05]. Junk Solutions Experts LLC uses a 100 or 250-mile radius and says shipping only happens if you arrange it with the seller; as they put it, while Kansas may have a great deal on a welder, they are not going to Kansas for a welder [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:03:39]. New GovDeals accounts are free but start on probation, capped at about three bids at a time, and the watch list counts against the same limit, so watch one unit and bid near the close; probation ends after three completed auctions, meaning bid, win, pick up [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:01:54]. On the federal side, JR finds trucks on autoauctions.gsa.gov, contacts the auction house running the sale, Metro AAA in Phoenix, emails the registration form with a driver's license scan, and receives an access code and bidder badge [14j6GQVGkBk @ 00:01:12]. Payment is due in 24 to 48 hours and pickup within 30 days, so line up funds and transport before you bid.

On the lot, UX Auctions runs a hands-on checklist: never check just one tire, expect drained batteries and check fuses, hunt for keys hidden in a door panel or under a mat, and always check the door sticker so the VIN and paint code match the listing [IUAs4NGQfyo @ 00:01:14]. They flag low brake fluid as a warning sign, check whether coolant was flushed, smell the oil and rub it between your fingers, and note that separately run aftermarket wiring pulls out cleanly because they ran their own wires. Auto Dealer Startup insists on scanning every car even at a dealer-clear sale, rejecting a 2019 unit outright because the OBD port was inoperable: I got to be able to pull that code on it [dzr9aYx98oY @ 00:11:30]. They also read a clear distance of zero as a sign the car sat or the battery died. Street Rat Garage sorts Chargers by sight, where recessed hubcaps mean AWD, and lists the carrier bearing as a common, easy DIY fix while listening for the Hemi tick from long idling [qieQr_fEJQ8 @ 00:02:04]. Before bidding, Top 5 Autos says pay the $12 to $15 fee for a VIN history [WFVGJDWST7I @ 00:04:44].

Pricing discipline comes from outside comps. JR sets a stop price from KBB before the sale and paid $13,000 plus $888 Arizona tax by credit card for an F-150 that carried an open recall, then pulled transport quotes of $780 for 650 miles or $1,400 for 2,200 miles [14j6GQVGkBk @ 00:02:42]. Junk Solutions Experts LLC checks Facebook Marketplace comps before buying anything, which is how they knew a $453 Durham fireproof cabinet would turn at about $775 within a week [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:10:43]. At the live Kesler Schaefer lane in Indianapolis, Street Rat Garage watches the screens: current bid is real money, asking means nobody has bid yet, a green flash marks an online bidder, and deals land either at the beginning when people are scared to bid or at the end when they run out of money [6chXsHCTJA4 @ 00:12:27]. Their own exit math on a 2008 Ram bought for about $1,396 with fees, where the check-engine light was a loose gas cap, is to list at $3,500 and accept $2,700 to $2,800 because Facebook Marketplace buyers negotiate down [cqTAqIJLC10 @ 00:28:32]. Build the bid backward from that realistic sale price, not from the sticker you post.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over when to pull the trigger. Top 5 Autos tells online buyers to snipe in the last 3-5 minutes of a GSA Auctions, GovPlanet, publicsurplus.com, or county sheriff listing [WFVGJDWST7I @ 00:05:35]. Street Rat Garage, watching GovDeals police Chargers close, calls that pointless: most bidders already sit on their hands until the end, and 'sniper bidding' buys nothing because every bid extends the clock, so the last-second ambush just resets the timer and invites a counter [qieQr_fEJQ8 @ 00:33:35]. Junk Solutions Experts LLC lands in the middle for a different reason. On a probation GovDeals account, bids and the watch list draw from the same roughly three-item limit, so they watch a single item and only bid near closing to avoid tying up slots on losers [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:03:58]. In a live lane the timing logic flips again. At the Kesler Schaefer police and seizure sale in Indianapolis, Street Rat Garage says the deals come either at the very beginning, when the room is scared to open, or at the very end, when buyers have run out of money, and a green flash on the screen means an online bidder just jumped in [6chXsHCTJA4 @ 00:12:27]. Late bidding is common ground; the fight is over whether the final seconds are an edge or just noise.

How deep the discount runs depends on who is talking. Top 5 Autos sells the goldmine version: over 25,000 vehicles a year, with seized units, repos, and fleet vehicles retired at 50-80K miles as the best hunting categories, plus case stories of a $55K SUV landing under $18K [WFVGJDWST7I @ 00:02:30]. Those case numbers wobble on a close read, with one Suburban quoted at both $14,500 and 14,000 before selling for $9,000. JR, who bought an F-150 by finding it on autoauctions.gsa.gov and registering with a Phoenix auction house, watched over 200 vehicles cross and saw only one go significantly below value, adding that dealers skip sales tax, so their disadvantage against retail buyers is smaller than it looks [14j6GQVGkBk @ 00:03:23]. Handyman Process, on a monthly San Antonio dealer lane running government whites and grays, clocked trucks at roughly $2-3k under retail, with 15-passenger vans still hammering at $22k-26k in 30-40 second runs against dealers, the public, and online bidders [FZRiWN_dcS4 @ 00:06:26]. East Coast Classics, after buying a couple dozen surplus cars, puts it bluntly: the deals exist, 'and those deals, they're few and far between' [g9Wt5wG1aGM @ 00:01:08]. The buyers who report firsthand numbers see thin spreads on clean late-model trucks; the fat margins sit in rough, cheap, or mechanically flawed units.

Practitioners also split on what to do with the unit once it is home. Tool Demos runs the fix-and-sell play: a $900 ex-fire-rescue and police Expedition, about 4 days of labor, junkyard console, rear hatch, and grille, police wiring stripped, black cladding flame-restored, and roughly $2,000 cash in against a KBB of $5,000-5,500, then sold below KBB to a friend [EFXJtp6q_B8 @ 00:08:56]. Street Rat Garage treats wrecked fleet units as parts inventory. On a frame-bent DNR van with 93K miles that hammered at $825 plus a fee they put at about 7%, the math was engine around $700, transmission around $600, and rear end $300-500 [qieQr_fEJQ8 @ 00:34:53]. Auto Dealer Startup rejects flipping as the main exit for cheap fleet-grade cars and rents them instead: a $2,500-3,500 economy car pulls $350-400 a week, the coach skips Teslas as off-strategy, and a partner bought a 301K-mile Camry for $700 and rents it for $350 a week [dzr9aYx98oY @ 00:18:04]. That fleet only takes Ford, Toyota, or Honda, while Dodge, Subaru, and Nissan Sentra get pushed to the flip pile [dzr9aYx98oY @ 00:12:53]. Same auction stock, three exits: repair and retail, part out, or weekly rental cash flow.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive surprises hide behind inspection limits. East Coast Classics lays out the preview ceiling: you can start the car, feel the brakes, engage the transmission, test HVAC, lights, and electrical, and plug in an OBD reader, 'and the biggest is you cannot drive the car,' with a fixed preview window and no makeup session, so the bid has to compensate for that blindness [g9Wt5wG1aGM @ 00:03:20]. Street Rat Garage reports the same wall on GovDeals: call ahead, start it, roll it forward and back, but no test drive and no shop inspection [cqTAqIJLC10 @ 00:08:33]. Tool Demos shows what slips through. The $900 Expedition was cheap because of an audible engine noise, and a scope capture referenced to cylinder 1 plus an amp-clamp relative compression test exposed a scored cylinder-3 exhaust cam lobe and a destroyed roller follower [EFXJtp6q_B8 @ 00:02:08]. Auto Dealer Startup refuses to bid blind on codes even in a dealer-clear lane, walking from a 2019 with an inoperable OBD port because 'I got to be able to pull that code on it,' and reading a clear distance of zero as a car that sat or had a dead battery [dzr9aYx98oY @ 00:11:30]. East Coast Classics' NJ State Police impound Jaguar, with a seized engine, blown brakes, and a leaking radiator, is the endpoint of skipping that discipline.

The second trap is the gap between hammer price and all-in cost. Junk Solutions Experts LLC won a school-district F-150 at $2,000 and was at $2,250 after buyer's premium and tax, warning 'that can take a little bit out of your profit' [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:13:42]. UX Auctions' 157,119-mile Southport fire department F-250 hammered at $4,150 after 47 bids and landed at $4,669 with fees [IUAs4NGQfyo @ 00:05:15]. Top 5 Autos pegs buyer premium at about 5% on GSA Auctions, up to 10% on GovPlanet, and up to 15% at sheriff auctions, plus $300-900 for transport [WFVGJDWST7I @ 00:08:09]. JR stacks the full bill on a long-distance buy: $13,000 for the F-150, $888 Arizona tax paid by credit card, transport quotes of $780 for 650 miles or $1,400 for 2,200 miles, a gate pass at pickup, and an extra 2% owed to New York because AZ-NY reciprocity applied. Without reciprocity, JR warns of double tax and filing DTF-804, DTF-802, and AU-11, and that truck also carried an open recall [14j6GQVGkBk @ 00:08:40]. On a $1,000-class fleet car, a 15% premium plus a transport bill can swallow most of the spread before a wrench turns, which is why every operator who posted real numbers quoted the all-in figure, not the hammer.

The last cluster is self-inflicted: bidding emotion and pickup logistics. Street Rat Garage watched a buyer drop a one-and-done $5,000 bid on a Carmel Explorer and overpay by about $600 when the next comparable unit went for $4,400, and warns to read the screens, because 'current bid' is real money while 'asking' means nobody has bid yet [6chXsHCTJA4 @ 00:10:04]. The same sale saw a seized Trackhawk hammer at $64,000 on a bill of sale with unknown miles, a number Street Rat Garage figured needed about $70k on resale to clear a profit [6chXsHCTJA4 @ 00:18:29]. Tool Demos' verdict on whether government auctions are worth it hinges on the same trap: 'You can definitely get into bidding wars with people and that's how the price gets out of control' [EFXJtp6q_B8 @ 00:09:31]. Junk Solutions Experts LLC adds the pickup squeeze: weekday-only pickup, a locked account and accruing storage if you no-show, and a seller who sat on marking an item picked up for about 1.5 weeks over Thanksgiving, which froze the speaker's probation bid slots until a call to GovDeals, because 'unless they mark that it's been picked up, Gov deals doesn't know' [El3cLMGi_9s @ 00:09:47]. Win at the right number, then have the weekday trailer run locked before the auction closes.

callout.title: Four checks before any fleet-vehicle bid goes in
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, overpay, or lockout a practitioner hit or watched happen in the lane.
items: Set a KBB-based stop price, then read the screen: 'current bid' is real money, 'asking' means nobody has bid [JR — 14j6GQVGkBk @ 00:02:42].

chapters.question_prompt: What do government surplus vehicles and equipment actually sell for at auction?
chapters.title: Sold-Price Walkthroughs: Real Hammer Prices From GSA and State Auctions
chapters.subtitle: Lot-by-lot prices for GSA pickups, vans, cars, and SUVs; county and city fleet vehicles; campers, trailers, boats, mowers, and generators; and the NH state surplus live auction day
chapters.executive_summary: Jeff of Auction Reviews With Jeff and Retired and Winging it, Sean Drake, and Cereal Marshmallows walk GSA, Florida county and state, and New Hampshire surplus lots and report what iron actually hammered for. Consensus: buy government-titled units over private consignment, because fleets retire on mileage or age with mandated maintenance, then inspect in person since everything sells as-is and often absolute. Street numbers: a 2018 Silverado at $6,750, 2014 and 2012 Chevys at $3,200, ex-cop Chargers and Impalas at $3,000 to $4,000, a 55,000-mile Merrimack unit at $6,500, Jeff's 2021 Explorer at $15,000 and their 2008 Malibu at $2,800. Fees swing from zero at the GSA Orlando sale to 2% on some agency lots. Friction points: Jeff leans toward GSA prices beating state sales, while Drake watched New Hampshire vehicles go sky high past their ceilings.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every walk-through lands on the same buy rule: government-titled iron first, private consignment last. Jeff, filming on Retired and Winging it, says they have never bought a private car off the Florida lot and always chase the state units first because they seem to be the best, while still calling every as-is purchase a gamble [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:01:23]. At a later Royal Auction sale Jeff is blunter: they would not buy a private unit from an auction at all, too risky, and they pass on company-branded work trucks because State of Florida cars are the ones that have always left them happy [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:48:56]. The logic is fleet rotation. Standing beside an F-350 dually on the GSA lot, Jeff explains agencies dump trucks because they hit a mileage or year limit, not because something broke, whereas private sellers often send cars to auction precisely because they have problems [cZOfyxWtGp8 @ 00:16:49]. Their own state career backs it up: vehicles had to go in for maintenance, records were kept, and supervisors called to chase anyone overdue [E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:23:14]. The upshot for an operator is a filter, not a preference: sort the lot by owner tag before you ever pop a door, and treat any unmarked, dealer, or private unit as a different risk class that has to be priced with a much wider safety margin.

The second point of agreement is that nobody should bid blind. At the Orlando GSA sale Jeff warns that buyers must collect the vehicle the day of the sale anyway, so they may as well walk it, because the auction house is prepping a lot full of cars and will never spend anywhere near the time a buyer would on one unit [E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:14:04]. On the county and state side Jeff pushes the Friday preview before the first-Saturday sale, when doors get unlocked, engines run, and buyers can confirm the AC blows cold [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:05:17]. Sean Drake, working the New Hampshire state surplus live day, shows the cost of skipping it: winners get their bid number taped to the windshield, and high bid numbers on units nobody started the day before tell you someone gambled without ever hearing the engine [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:04:06]. Jeff's own Royal Auction walk shows why the preview pays: one of the few trucks that finally cranked had been smoked in and was making a sound, exactly the kind of defect that never shows up in a listing photo [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:12:53]. The practitioners run a funnel: build the list online, cross units off in person, and bid only on the survivors that start, shift, smell clean, and match the written condition notes posted on the glass.

Third, the practitioners treat sold-price history as the real weapon. Walking a row of Elantras, Jeff points out that the same models come back sale after sale, so a car you missed will reappear, and knowing past hammer prices tells you both when a lot is running too hot and roughly what to bid [Vi6nU6UkkoQ @ 00:11:28]. That discipline matters because these are no-safety-net fights: at the Florida county sale Jeff reminds viewers it is an absolute auction where the high bidder takes the unit no matter what [6-YX9_QfY1A @ 00:08:57]. Jeff frames the format as an advantage once the homework is done, listing no pressure at all, picking exactly what you want, and stopping wherever your price ends [gIFFMdh2fBk @ 00:02:27]. Sean Drake adds the emotional brake from the New Hampshire floor: after watching a small military trailer go for $200 and wondering whether a $250 bid would have taken it, they conclude you have to be careful not to go crazy at live sales and should only buy what you actually need or can make money on [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:10:29]. The working agreement is simple: price book first, ceiling second, and walk away content when the room outruns your number, because the same unit type rolls through the gate again at the next monthly sale.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The hard numbers come from Jeff's results boards and Sean Drake's live floor. At one Florida government sale Jeff reads off a cluster of pickups: a 2018 Chevrolet Silverado at $6,750, a 2014 Silverado and a 2012 Chevrolet each at $3,200, a 2015 Silverado at $4,200, a 2007 Dodge Ram at $4,800, and a 2011 Ram 1500 at $3,800 [P82Ir2OeO50 @ 00:01:43]. In New Hampshire, Drake clocks the old state police fleet: Impalas going for $3,000 plus and Chargers and other ex-cop units landing at $3,000 to $4,000, all carrying heavy idle time that bidders forget to price in [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:03:12]. A Town of Merrimack unit with 55,000 miles that only needed a jump climbed through rapid-fire increments and sold at $6,500 [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:07:24]. Jeff's own buys set the retail-grade benchmark: a 2021 Explorer with under 50,000 miles, brand new tires, and a clean dash at $15,000, which they call a really good car that runs perfect [YaIalHq0RVU @ 01:06:59]. Read together, the spread is wide: tired late-model pickups and ex-patrol sedans cluster in the low thousands, while low-mile, late-model SUVs command mid-teens money, so the price book has to be segmented by model year, mileage band, and former duty, whether patrol, work truck, or administrative car, before any comparison means anything.

Cost structure shifts by venue, and the practitioners spell it out. Jeff's GSA sale at Orlando Auto Auction, a General Services Administration contract holder, charges no buyer fees, which they call really good, but the catch is that the winning bidder has to pick the vehicle up the day of the sale [E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:13:44]. On the Florida county and state lot Jeff flags the opposite: some units carry a 2% buyer fee on the amount paid, apparently depending on the selling agency, so the same winning bid can land at different all-in costs [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:24:48]. Format varies too. At the Royal Auction sale the auctioneer works from a tent, showing the lot number while bidders call from their seats instead of following a truck around the yard, and Jeff notes very few people bidding under that tent, very few online, and far fewer cars than at other sales they attend [YaIalHq0RVU @ 01:06:36]. That thin crowd is the opening. After their second GSA sale Jeff says the prices looked pretty decent and probably better than the state auctions they usually work, while admitting the full analysis was not finished [cZOfyxWtGp8 @ 00:08:40]. An operator should weigh both the fee line and the number of live paddles in the room before deciding which venue gets the bankroll this month.

The field kit is cheap. Sitting in a 2019 F-150 XLT on the GSA lot, Jeff tells serious buyers to pull the codes before bidding, noting a scanner can be had for under $100 [E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:21:53]. Road tests are off the table: at the GSA preview you can crank a unit, run it through the gears, and back it up a few feet, but you cannot drive it, so the shift feel and cold-start sound carry the whole verdict [2Zb68VFEJ1c @ 00:22:52]. Post-purchase conversion is the hidden line item on ex-police iron. Walking a row of Tahoes, Jeff explains you have to strip the glue and plug the spotlight hole with a grommet, and they deliberately hunt units that never wore a spotlight or decals, adding that decals come off clean as long as nobody scratched the paint during removal [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:06:52]. On a City of Clearwater Explorer they show the failure case: whoever pulled the decals nicked the paint, which turns a goo-remover job into a paint job [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:37:56]. Budget those fixes before the hammer drops, because a scuffed decal outline, a missing console, or an open spotlight hole all erode the spread between your winning bid and what the unit is actually worth parked in a driveway or listed for resale.

callout.title: Edges the lot-walkers use to buy under the room
callout.body: Small reads on timing, tires, wiring, and body damage that the practitioners use to spot value or dodge a hidden fix.
items: Time the calendar: from Jeff's experience prices tend to run a little lower at the end of the year, November and December and sometimes October, so they flag a December sale as a buying window [Auction Reviews With Jeff — iauTGRI39kE @ 00:11:24].

Read the rubber: Jeff says tires in really good shape usually mark a government unit, because agencies carry a maintenance budget and keep tires replaced [Auction Reviews With Jeff — 3ej4xfd_ers @ 00:04:48].

Check the ports on ex-police Tahoes: Jeff found the USB connections disconnected, likely from the police equipment wiring, and reconnecting them still did not restore charging [Auction Reviews With Jeff — J-UWth-6Hd0 @ 00:21:42].
Target the dinged-but-clean unit: Jeff expects a Tahoe with a little body damage to hammer lower than its identical clean siblings in the same row [Retired and Winging it — pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:19:47].

sop_steps.title: Build the sold-price book
sop_steps.action: Log hammer prices by model, year, mileage, and former duty across every monthly sale.
sop_steps.detail: Jeff stresses that the same models return sale after sale, so past prices tell you when a lot is running too high and what to bid [Auction Reviews With Jeff — Vi6nU6UkkoQ @ 00:11:28], and they point buyers back to earlier videos for what identical Pacifica vans sold for [Auction Reviews With Jeff — KAvziIIGe68 @ 00:01:30].

sop_steps.title: Shortlist online, cut in person
sop_steps.action: Pick candidates from the listing, then strike units at the preview until only bid-worthy survivors remain.
sop_steps.detail: Jeff arrives with a few picks, marks some off as nope once they see them in person, and bids only on what is left [Auction Reviews With Jeff — E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:14:22]; on the Florida county lot that cut happens at the Friday preview before the first-Saturday sale [Retired and Winging it — pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:05:17].

sop_steps.title: Run the no-drive field test
sop_steps.action: Scan codes, crank, cycle the gears, back up a few feet, and ask staff to jump dead units.
sop_steps.detail: Jeff carries a code scanner that costs under $100 [Auction Reviews With Jeff — E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:21:53], tests by cranking and backing up since driving is not allowed [Auction Reviews With Jeff — 2Zb68VFEJ1c @ 00:22:52], and notes staff will jump non-cranking units if you wait [Auction Reviews With Jeff — YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:04:09].

sop_steps.title: Hold the ceiling and plan pickup
sop_steps.action: Write a hard ceiling per lot, stop at it, and arrange same-day removal before bidding.
sop_steps.detail: Sean Drake held a just-under-$2,000 ceiling on a Ranger that went for $2,750 [Sean Drake — ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:02:13], and at the GSA Orlando sale the winner must pick the vehicle up the day of the sale [Auction Reviews With Jeff — E3mh6G6h8zM @ 00:13:44].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is which lot actually prints cheap iron. On the federal side, Jeff of Auction Reviews With Jeff came off a second GSA sale at Orlando Auto Auction calling the hammer prices pretty decent and, with the full analysis still pending, likely better than the Florida state auctions Jeff normally works [cZOfyxWtGp8 @ 00:08:40]. On the Retired and Winging It channel, Jeff's own purchases come from state and local lots instead: a 2008 Florida agency Malibu bought for 2,800 dollars and driven for several years [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:11:06], and a 2005 Florida Wildlife Commission F-150 4x4 bought for about 8,588 when comparable trucks were going for 12,000 to 14,000 [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:22:10]. Sean Drake's New Hampshire state surplus day reads the opposite way on price: by mid-auction the vehicles were going sky high, with Impalas running around 3,000 dollars and the old state police units clearing three to four thousand [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:02:54]. Drake's crowd was also aggressive on the ground, sitting on the units they wanted and signaling everyone else not to bother. The takeaway is that no single lane is reliably cheap. The GSA lane, the Florida state-and-local lane, and the New England state lane each behave differently, and each needs its own logged comps before a bid card goes up on anything.

Seller pedigree is the second fault line. Jeff draws a hard line at government fleet units: walking a Royal Auction Group lot, Jeff passed on a private 2019 Challenger flat out, saying a private unit bought from an auction is too risky and that it just would not happen [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:48:56]. The logic comes from the GSA yard, where Jeff argues federal units retire because they hit a mileage or years threshold, while private consignors often send cars to auction precisely because something is wrong with them [cZOfyxWtGp8 @ 00:17:14]. Cereal Marshmallows works a looser playbook built around rarity rather than run-and-drive certainty, framing state surplus as equipment that is good enough for an entrepreneur even after it is no longer good enough for the government [RvlA07ePLd4 @ 00:00:30]. The top target on that walk was an '89 Caprice cop car with no rust and all its trim, tagged no start, and the read was that a no-start on a Chevy cannot be all that big of a deal [RvlA07ePLd4 @ 00:05:41]. Two playbooks fall out of this. Jeff's model is to buy the cleanest retired fleet unit on the lot, where certainty is the margin. The project-hunter model bets that a disclosed defect scares off the crowd and opens the gap.

Ex-police units split the field again. On the Retired and Winging It channel, Jeff describes running former Florida Highway Patrol 5.0 Mustangs for years, calling them the funnest cars ever driven, and selling them for at least what was in them [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:17:50]. The same walk carries the counterweight: buy the unit with the least modification possible, because an early Crown Vic purchase still wore the bumblebee yellow-and-black FHP scheme and had to go out for paint [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:09:33]. At the Royal lot, Jeff softens that rule, noting a spotlight can be pulled and the hole plugged, a trim panel swapped, and decals stripped so cleanly nobody can tell they were there, unless the agency crew scratched the paint on the way off [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:41:24]. Sean Drake's live New Hampshire read adds the number every police-unit bidder has to price in: old state cruisers at three to four thousand dollars, with the warning that a lot of them carry heavy idle time that bidders should not forget [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:03:12]. So one camp hunts the cleanest, least-modified unit on the lot and accepts paying up for it. The other camp buys marked cruisers and budgets from day one for paint, plugs, panels, and idle-hour wear.

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated firsthand failure is a unit that looks right and runs wrong. At the GSA preview, Jeff cranked one Ford Fusion that made the same bad startup noise as an earlier Fusion and did not smell good, then cranked a second Fusion that started silently and smelled clean, and drew the lesson directly: that gap is exactly why buyers have to get out to the lot and check these units in person [Vi6nU6UkkoQ @ 00:26:47]. Even then the test is limited; Jeff notes the best case would be a drive down the road, but the yard will not allow it, so the check stops at sitting in it, cranking it, and opening every door [Vi6nU6UkkoQ @ 00:27:10]. At the Royal Auction Group lot, unit after unit refused to crank, which Jeff chalks up to vehicles sitting so long, adding that staff will jump them off if you wait [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:06:45]. Sean Drake watched the downside play out live: bid numbers went on windshields after each sale, and some high bidders had never shown up the day before to start the vehicle, which turned those buys into a real gamble [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:04:06]. The economics check is blunt. A no-crank or rough-crank unit gets priced as a mechanical unknown, never as a running vehicle with a quick fix.

Condition sheets catch some damage and miss some. Jeff warns that a lot of units on the Florida state and local lot carry hurricane water damage, and that the agencies note it, or at least are supposed to [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:28:58]. Flood risk cuts both ways on price: at Royal, a 2022 Ford with 6,257 miles was tagged flood damaged and rebuildable, yet Jeff predicted it would still bring a pretty good price because it looked almost brand new [YaIalHq0RVU @ 00:19:06]. That is the trap in plain view: the cosmetics pull bidders up while the disclosure says the water got in. Disclosures on the big municipal lots are blunt when they exist; on one walk Jeff read a Transit van tag listing a fuel leak and bad soft brakes [P82Ir2OeO50 @ 00:16:01]. Cereal Marshmallows hit the paperwork side of the same problem, passing on trailers that came with a mold disclosure buyers had to sign before taking them [RvlA07ePLd4 @ 00:09:27]. The operating rule from these walks is to treat the written disclosure as the floor of what is wrong, not the ceiling. Read the tag first, then run the smell and listen checks on any unit that might have taken water, and price the worst case before the lot number comes up in the tent.

The economics failures come down to bid discipline. Sean Drake let a small military trailer go at 200 dollars after debating a 250 bid, then laid out the rule: be careful at live sales not to go a little crazy, and only buy something you actually need or can make money on [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:10:15]. Drake also held a hard ceiling earlier in the day, watching a little Ranger hammer at 2,750 when the personal number was just under 2,000 [ovCY1VA7klw @ 00:02:13]. Jeff's version is about defect pricing: a unit tagged smokes is only worth buying for someone with a shop, who is sure of the fix, and who gets it at a very low price [pl4wTzpNWRQ @ 00:10:20]. Hidden upfit costs show up after the hammer too; trying to charge a dead phone, Jeff found the USB ports on former police Tahoes disconnected and still dead after reconnecting, blamed the police equipment that had been wired in, and flagged it as something to watch on any ex-police buy [J-UWth-6Hd0 @ 00:21:42]. Every one of these is a margin leak: emotional overbids on units nobody needed, uncapped repair risk on disclosed defects, and upfit damage that nobody prices in until the unit is already home and sitting in the driveway.

callout.title: Hard Stops Before The Bid Card Goes Up

chapters.question_prompt: How do I buy heavy equipment and military machinery at online and on-site auctions without getting burned?
chapters.title: Heavy Equipment and IronPlanet: Bidding on Iron
chapters.subtitle: IronPlanet online bidding and inspection guarantees, government sold prices for excavators, skid steers, and dump trucks, equipment-auction mistakes, aging-inventory liquidation, military forklifts, and on-site asset viewings
chapters.executive_summary: Operators buying government and fleet iron agree the profit is locked in at the hammer, not at resale. Casey LaDelle preaches hard bid limits, worst-case leak math, and skipping MaxForce trucks. Quentin of Iron King Inc. shows GovPlanet military trucks bought for $800 to $9,000, with the $9,000 LVSR swelling to $25,000 to $30,000 once missing ECUs and parts land. IronPlanet pitches inspected iron left at the seller's site, roughly 15 bids per item from over 130 countries, no-reserve live bidding, and a Make Offer channel where offers exceed prior bids. Dave Doing Things counters that the offer haggle felt like getting played, yet it closed around $9,100. Auction Reviews With Jeff logs hours and lot numbers on county and state fleet sales, while Welding and Wheeling grabs $3 to $300 small-iron flips.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who actually writes checks for iron lands on the same rule: the money is made at the purchase, not at resale. Casey LaDelle puts it flat, 'You make money by buying it for a good price,' and backs it with a hard warning about auction-floor ego: 'you need to have your limit and make it a hard limit,' because chasing a lot 'one more time' has cost buyers tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:13:50] [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:19:24]. Quentin of Iron King Inc. frames the same math from the military side, saying 'you can get awesome deals if you're prepared to work on the piece of equipment,' which means the discount only exists for buyers who can wrench, source parts, and absorb downtime [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:27:21]. Welding and Wheeling applies the rule in real time on a Clark 825 skid loader in Brown Town, Wisconsin: after finding dark, overfull engine oil, low coolant, and a sludgy top end, the verdict was that 'this thing's going to have to go cheap for me to screw with it' [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:41:28]. The consensus price discipline is simple and brutal: the defect list sets the ceiling, and that ceiling does not move once the auctioneer starts working the crowd and the bidding gets emotional.

The second point of agreement is that surplus iron leaves the fleet for a reason, and buyers should price it that way from the first walk-around. Quentin states it bluntly, 'The military would never get rid of a good working vehicle,' and shows LVSR and MTVR units routinely arriving with ECUs, doors, and cab monitors robbed to keep other trucks in service [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:25:40]. Welding and Wheeling says the same about civilian iron, noting that 'a skid loader like this doesn't get parked for no reason,' even when the hydrostatic oil looks clean and the auxiliaries work [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 01:01:12]. Auction Reviews With Jeff shows how openly municipal sellers flag trouble: lot 178 'turns over with jump, does not start,' and other county units carry disclosed hydraulic leaks and five-figure hour meters right on the listing [HQ3YV3h4sC4 @ 00:04:12]. Casey LaDelle closes the loop on unknown leaks, warning that a drip could be a cheap O-ring or a roughly $10,000 valve body, so the only safe move is to assume the worst and drop the bid cap to match [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:13:36]. Disclosed defects are not hidden traps; they are line items the bidder must subtract before the first raise, and the operators who skip that subtraction end up owning somebody else's problem.

On the platform side, IronPlanet's own pitch and the street buyers agree on the baseline prerequisites: register early, read the inspection package, and understand that the hammer is final. IronPlanet says most equipment is inspected under IronClad Assurance and stays at the seller's site, which avoids transport costs, and its inspections include fluid samples and 35 to 50 photos backed by a 'make you whole' guarantee [KyKSH6vNrZ8 @ 00:00:36] [rsMWDCVh1cE @ 00:01:34]. Its live-bid walkthrough tells buyers to register in advance, place priority bids early, and accept that the highest bidder wins 'no matter what the price,' with no time extensions and no reserves [-1B3hGKjbz0 @ 00:01:05]. Auction Reviews With Jeff runs the price-discovery side by hand, walking state and county yards and later matching sold prices to item numbers so viewers 'know what you might have to spend' before the next sale comes around [rDFBP32Mq2I @ 00:00:00]. The working consensus is that inspection reports and sold-price history are the homework. Buyers who skip either one are bidding blind against a global crowd that already did its research, and in a no-reserve format there is no second chance to walk back a number once the auctioneer calls it sold.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Iron King's numbers show exactly how a cheap hammer price turns into real money. Quentin bought a 2010 LVSR 10x10 with a C15, Allison, and hooklift out of Yermo, California for $9,000, then found the suspension and ABS ECUs missing; Oshkosh has discontinued the ECU, and a replacement runs $10,000 'if you can even find one,' pushing the total to $25,000 to $30,000 or leaving a '9 to $10,000 paperweight' [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:06:27]. The MTVR cost $4,400 as a non-runner against roughly $7,000 for runners, but 90 to 95 percent sell without doors, windshield, or turret cap, and replacements cost $6,000 for doors from a single maker, $500 for glass, and $400 for the turret cap [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:20:47]. Add $10,000 to $12,000 in tires and that truck lands near $26,000 [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:24:22]. Scratch Fab's GovPlanet military forklift, a likely 1976 silent hoist rated at 10,000 lb with about 980 hours, exposes the pickup-day costs nobody lists: no oil in the engine, a hydraulic system needing about 20 gallons when only 10 were brought, a hot-wired ignition, no brakes, and a reserved trailer whose removable gooseneck was too tall, which cost hours on site [45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:20:30].

Casey LaDelle's lot walk is a running checklist of where value hides and where it leaks out. On a 3,500-gallon fuel and lube conversion, confirm the product pumps and valves are still there, because boneyards rob them, and the hose reels, pumps, and valves can be worth more than the truck itself, which makes a part-out play viable [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:04:29]. Any truck with a MaxForce engine is a hard skip for resale, since lenders refuse to finance them; the exception is a part-out, like the blower truck bought around $10,000 where the body sells for $10,000 and the roughly $5,000 cab-chassis is the profit [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:39:09]. Fresh, shiny DOT tape signals a recent respray, and on lowboys the 8/12/8 tire layout means tens of thousands of dollars in rubber, so tread condition swings trailer value hard [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:10:12]. Welding and Wheeling adds the hour-meter check: the sale bill on a Clark 825 claimed 10,000 hours while the meter read 981, so the buyer looked for evidence of a rollover before trusting either number, then pulled the valve cover and found sludge [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:39:43]. Every one of these checks takes minutes on preview day and can save five figures at the hammer.

IronPlanet's mechanics reward buyers who set their numbers before the sale starts. Its walkthrough sells items by lot number with no time slots; priority bids placed early fire automatically, the auctioneer replays them and lowers the ask when nobody bids, and choice groups let the winner take one or more similar units at the final price [-1B3hGKjbz0 @ 00:00:27]. The company's webinar team describes the Make Offer side: sellers accept, counter, or reject, set a threshold that filters out a '$20' joke offer, and buyers get 48 hours to answer a counter, which can be done on mobile [rn9oCm5t39A @ 00:50:07]. Dave Doing Things ran that channel on a rusty 2015 Silverado with 82,000 km listed at 14,500: an opening $10,000 offer, an IronPlanet call asking for more, a suspicious $11,000 rival, a sold tag, a relist, a drop to $8,000, then $9,000, finally closing with the seller absorbing the 10 percent fee so the truck shows sold at $10,000 while Dave pays about $9,100 [8FXm7sOaFwg @ 00:02:52]. Settlement runs through a secure account, the seller releases to the buyer's transporter, and the full cycle takes four to five weeks, so haul-out scheduling belongs in the plan [KyKSH6vNrZ8 @ 00:01:46].
