callout.title: Preview-Day Tells That Separate a Buy From a Paperweight
callout.body: These are the fast physical checks and sourcing moves the buyers use to spot cosmetic cover-ups and kill parts costs before and after the hammer.
items: Crawl under and check the unpainted underside for the 'Richie Brothers overhaul,' because Ritchie paints for a percentage and fresh paint up top proves nothing [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:19:39]
Treat new, shiny DOT tape as proof of a fresh respray and look harder at what the paint is covering [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:10:12]
Hunt Marketplace for discontinued military parts: a $4,000 CAT ECM turned up for $600, and the $400 14/28V regulators are worth hoarding [iron king productions — vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:21:19]
Distrust spray-in bed liner on service trucks, because it hides festering rust, as seen on an '04 6.0L with 168,000 miles [Welding and Wheeling — UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:04:19]

sop_steps.title: Register Early and Log Every Lot
sop_steps.action: Register before the sale, place priority bids early, and record lot numbers for later sold-price matching.
sop_steps.detail: IronPlanet sells by lot number with no time slots, and priority bids placed early bid automatically [IronPlanet — -1B3hGKjbz0 @ 00:00:27]; Jeff reads lot numbers aloud so sold prices can be matched afterward [Auction Reviews With Jeff — HQ3YV3h4sC4 @ 00:05:25].

sop_steps.title: Inspect the Physical Tells
sop_steps.action: Pull the valve cover, check fluid levels, and compare the hour meter against the sale bill for rollover.
sop_steps.detail: On the Clark 825, the engine oil was overfull and dark, coolant was low, and the top end was sludgy, contradicting the clean hydrostatic oil [Welding and Wheeling — UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:41:07].

sop_steps.title: Build the Landed-Cost Cap
sop_steps.action: Add missing parts, tires, shipping, and worst-case leak repairs to the hammer price before setting the cap.
sop_steps.detail: The $4,400 MTVR climbed to about $26,000 once $10,000 to $12,000 in tires joined the doors, glass, and turret cap [iron king productions — vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:24:22].

sop_steps.title: Bid to a Hard Limit and Arrive Ready to Haul
sop_steps.action: Stop at the written ceiling, then show up with fluids, batteries, and a trailer confirmed to fit the machine.
sop_steps.detail: Casey insists the limit must be 'a hard limit' [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:19:24]; Scratch Fab lost hours when the reserved trailer's removable gooseneck was too tall [Scratch Fab — 45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:21:13].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The no-reserve question splits the IronPlanet camp itself. The IronPlanet bidding tutorial lays down the hard rule: the highest bidder wins "no matter what the price," with no time extensions and no reserves [-1B3hGKjbz0 @ 00:01:05]. CMO Matt Aley backs that on the IronPlanet Marketing webinar, arguing reserve auctions "turn off buyers" and drag down engagement [rn9oCm5t39A @ 00:36:11]. Yet the IronPlanet buy-and-sell pitch still lists reserve auctions inside the daily marketplace, next to featured, one-owner and private branded dealer formats [rsMWDCVh1cE @ 00:03:01]. The alternative is Make Offer, where the seller accepts, counters or rejects. Dave Doing Things shows how that feels from the buyer's chair. Dave offered $10,000 on a rusty 2015 Silverado listed at 14,500, got a call asking them to go higher, watched a rival $11,000 offer appear, saw the truck marked sold and then relisted, and said "I had the feeling I was getting played" [8FXm7sOaFwg @ 00:01:48]. Dave dropped to $8,000, came back at $9,000, and closed with the seller absorbing the 10% fee, paying about $9,100. Operators who want certainty bid the no-reserve ring; operators who can handle phone pressure work the offer channel and lowball on purpose.

Buying unseen is the second fault line. IronPlanet's own pitch says its inspections, with fluid samples and 35 to 50 photos, give buyers the confidence to buy a "$200,000 bulldozer" without walking it [rsMWDCVh1cE @ 00:01:16]. Quentin of iron king productions bought an $800 LMTV out of Hawaii the remote way, and once fees and $5,000 shipping landed, Quentin noted "there's $6,000 there, and I haven't even seen the truck in person yet" [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:07:14]. The walk-the-yard crowd works differently. Welding and Wheeling crawled a Clark 825 skid loader whose sale bill claimed 10,000 hours while the meter read 981, then checked whether the meter had rolled over before trusting either number [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:39:43]. AuctionHub SA, viewing construction and mining assets for clients, found truck tractors and trailers displayed coupled together but sold separately, a layout called "quite confusing" until you get the hang of it [zEvheNxg0WE @ 00:01:43]. The split is plain: the platform sells inspection reports and a "make you whole" guarantee as a substitute for travel, while yard-walkers treat the physical walk-around, the valve cover and the hour meter as the real inspection and price only what they personally touched.

The third split is whether a dead or tired machine is opportunity or warning. Quentin at iron king productions buys non-runners on purpose and sums up the thesis bluntly: "You can get awesome deals if you're prepared to work on the piece of equipment" [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:27:21]. Scratch Fab proved the upside on a GovPlanet military forklift: no oil in the engine, a hot-wired ignition, a bypassed fuel pump, and by day's end "it drives" [45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:19:14]. Welding and Wheeling read the same signals the other way on a Clark skid loader with sludge under the valve cover: "a skid loader like this doesn't get parked for no reason," so it had to go cheap or not at all [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 01:01:12]. Volume strategy splits the same way. Welding and Wheeling scooped a $25 snowblower to flip at first snow and a $30 four-wheeler for parts, while Casey LaDelle walks past small and van trailers because at roughly $1,000 there is no margin left [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:45:04]. Quentin also concedes "the military would never get rid of a good working vehicle," which is why runners bring about $7,000 while Quentin's non-runner MTVR went for $4,400.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap on government iron is what is missing, not what is broken. Quentin at iron king productions paid GovPlanet $9,000 for a 2010 LVSR hooklift and warns these units often arrive missing the suspension and ABS ECUs; Oshkosh discontinued them, and "they've been robbed for other trucks to be put back into service," leaving a $10,000 part "if you can even find one" [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:03:17]. Without them, the truck risks becoming a "9 to $10,000 paperweight." The MTVR followed the same pattern: 90 to 95% sell without doors, windshield or turret cap, and the doors alone run $6,000 from a single maker [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:20:30]. Casey LaDelle sees the boneyard version on fuel and lube trucks, where product pumps and valves get "robbed," and those reels, pumps and valves can be worth more than the machine itself [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:04:29]. Scratch Fab's forklift arrived with no oil in the engine, and its damaged gas tank was replaced with a temporary plastic marine tank [45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:04:05]. The economics check is a parts census before the bid: list every module, door, cap and pump that should be on the unit, price what is gone, and subtract it from your cap.

Landed cost on surplus iron runs far past the hammer price. Quentin's $800 LMTV became about $1,000 with fees, then $6,000 after $5,000 shipping, before four 6TL batteries at $200 to $300 each, a $400 discontinued regulator, and close to $1,000 in cab bushings and airbags [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:07:14]. The $4,400 MTVR climbed to about $26,000 once $10,000 to $12,000 in tires landed, and a bad engine pushes the bill to about $30,000 [vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:24:22]. Casey LaDelle's Landoll trailer is the cautionary tale: the auction hid defects, projected profit was $20,000 and actual profit came in around $280 [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:04:09]. On lowboys, Casey warns of a $70,000 repair bill on an Aspen 9-axle and an 8/12/8 tire layout worth tens of thousands, adding "tires make a huge difference in the value of the trailer because there's so many of them" [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:50:54]. Unknown leaks get the same conservative treatment from Casey: a weep could be an O-ring or a roughly $10,000 valve body, so assume the worst and drop your cap. Casey's rule cuts through all of it: "You make money by buying it for a good price."

Discipline and logistics are where the rest of the money leaks out. Casey LaDelle says "one more time" bidding has cost tens to hundreds of thousands and insists "you need to have your limit and make it a hard limit" [XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:19:24]. Welding and Wheeling admitted the opposite drift after a packed Brown Town sale: "I spent a lot more than I usually do, and I ended up with a lot more than I usually do" [UpuweWTtiG4 @ 01:10:30]. Getting iron home is its own failure mode. Scratch Fab's forklift had no brakes, stopped only by shifting into the opposite gear, needed full throttle to move, and the reserved trailer's removable gooseneck was too tall, burning hours [45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:20:30]. Welding and Wheeling hauled about 6,500 lb plus extra gear at 55 to 60 mph and watched EGTs run high enough to need an intercooler. AuctionHub SA hit dead batteries on the yard, depleted "completely," and had to fetch more powerful batteries just to start the machines [zEvheNxg0WE @ 00:00:22]. Even the paperwork misleads: Auction Reviews With Jeff found no catalog at one state sale and warned that among those lots "some of these are state owned... some aren't." Budget the trailer, batteries, fluids and hours before you budget the bid.

callout.title: Kill the Bid If Any of These Checks Fail
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss, overrun or near-miss an operator took firsthand on surplus heavy iron.
items: Run a missing-parts census on military trucks: ECUs, doors, glass and turret caps get robbed, and the doors alone cost $6,000 [iron king productions — vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:20:30].
Price every unknown leak as the worst case, a roughly $10,000 valve body rather than an O-ring, and lower your cap to match [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:13:36].
Cross-check the hour meter against the sale bill and look under the valve cover; sludge means the machine goes cheap or not at all [Welding and Wheeling — UpuweWTtiG4 @ 00:41:28].
Confirm brakes, trailer deck height and gooseneck clearance before pickup day so loading does not eat hours [Scratch Fab — 45dQRk6d9Sw @ 00:20:30].

chapters.pull_quote: "You can get awesome deals if you're prepared to work on the piece of equipment." — attributed to iron king productions (vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:27:21).
action_checklist: Set a hard maximum before the ring opens and refuse "one more time" raises [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 01:19:24].
Register in advance and place priority max bids early so they bid automatically when the auctioneer replays them [IronPlanet — -1B3hGKjbz0 @ 00:00:27].

On Make Offer listings, walk your number down when rival offers look staged; Dave Doing Things closed at about $9,100 with the seller absorbing the 10% fee [Dave Doing Things — 8FXm7sOaFwg @ 00:02:52].
Look up a fleet seller's FMCSA inspections and check the unpainted underside for a fresh respray [Casey LaDelle — XAvSq6gx5KQ @ 00:19:39].
On every newly bought military truck, change all fluids, start a log book and grease every zerk [iron king productions — vlBL3apKXg0 @ 00:09:49].
Record lot numbers on the walk-through and match them to sold prices afterward to build your own price book [Auction Reviews With Jeff — HQ3YV3h4sC4 @ 00:05:25].

chapters.question_prompt: What is the real process of buying a surplus Humvee on GovPlanet, from bidding through pickup?
chapters.title: The GovPlanet Humvee Purchase
chapters.subtitle: Account setup and bidding, what to avoid in listings, rising auction prices, scam concerns, GovPlanet versus Facebook Marketplace, Yermo pickup releases, trailering home, and first-start attempts on M1097R1 and M1114 units
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners who have bought, hauled, and wrenched on GovPlanet Humvees agree on the core loop: get approved to bid, buy semi sight unseen off detailed photos and a limited function check, clear an end-use certificate that runs from 12 weeks to half a year, and insist on an SF-97 for street legal paperwork. The street mechanics are hard numbers: priority bids climb in $100 steps, five-minute closes double or triple prices, and 30-second overtimes pushed one buyer from $9,500 to $12,500. A $10,200 win invoiced at $12,290.40, and broker shipping ran $850 from Georgia to Missouri. Screening keys on 6.5 overdrive trucks, zero blow-by, and wear on pedals and switches. The split: Kevin24Seven now leans toward Facebook Marketplace after watching GovPlanet trucks clear $35,000 to $50,000, while Rasmussen Equipment pulled a near-new non-runner that only needed batteries.

key_metrics.label: All-In Invoice On A $10,200 Win
key_metrics.context: Kevin24Seven's GovPlanet invoice after winning at $10,200, built from a $1,030 transaction fee and a $50 SF-97 fee, before shipping.

key_metrics.label: Overtime Extension Price Creep
key_metrics.context: Kevin24Seven thought the auction was won at about $9,500, then repeated 30-second extensions forced the final win at $12,500.

key_metrics.label: End-Use Certificate Clearance Wait
key_metrics.value: Up to 12 weeks (all 12 used, October to January)
key_metrics.context: Split Builds bought a Marine Corps Humvee in October and the EUC did not clear for pickup until January.

key_metrics.label: Broker Transport Cost
key_metrics.value: $850 Albany, Georgia to St. Louis, Missouri
key_metrics.context: Kevin24Seven's driver through broker LTI Delivers hauled the truck for about $850; Kevin24Seven puts the typical range at $500 to $1,200 by distance.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every buyer who has actually closed a GovPlanet Humvee describes the same front gate: build an account, request buying privileges, and get cleared before a single bid counts. Split Builds walks through it as entering basic info and a credit card that sits uncharged unless you win and fail to pay, with privileges granted inside roughly 24 hours [CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:00:20]. Kevin24Seven had a rougher ride: the approval took a week or two, and GovPlanet's system flagged them as living in Canada until a phone call fixed it [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:02:07]. Their standing advice is to call the contact number, expect long hold times, and lean on staff who are understaffed but genuinely helpful [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:01:09]. MotorTrend's Dirt Every Day host frames the same step as signing up, getting a bidder number, and watching the rolling auction calendar [Wg0ziRtQ9JM @ 00:00:53]. Once inside, the shared reality is that you buy semi sight unseen. You cannot touch, start, or drive the truck; you get a written condition report plus dozens of high-detail photos covering interior, exterior, under the hood, and undercarriage. Kevin24Seven counted 82 photos on a single listing and warns to assume more is wrong than the limited function check admits [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:03:13].

The second point of total agreement is the paperwork tail. Winning is not owning: the buyer submits an end-use certificate, GovPlanet reviews it and forwards it to the branch that ran the truck, and that branch runs what Split Builds calls a mini background check before release [CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:01:49]. Split Builds says it can take up to 12 weeks and theirs burned all 12, buying in October and not getting clearance until January. Kevin24Seven tells first-timers to expect a good two to three months, maybe more, with the truck sitting untouchable in the lot the entire time [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:10:40]. By 2024 the same operator was warning buyers to brace for five to nine months, possibly longer [TLQhxsY7JoE @ 00:07:05]. Behind the EUC sits the SF-97. Kevin24Seven calls it really important for getting the truck street legal and insists you confirm the listing sells with one, noting that in Missouri it functions sort of like a title; it landed in the mailbox roughly four to five months after purchase [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:12:42]. Midwestern Garage paid a little extra to have GovPlanet issue an actual title rather than the bare SF-97, reasoning that letting them handle it saves time [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:08:45].

The third consensus point: whatever you win shows up stripped, dead, and partially robbed. HHWheels, hauling a friend's truck out of Albany, Georgia, found it extremely bare bones, with no batteries, no armor, and every military-related item pulled [09UUwyLab_0 @ 00:03:17]. Midwestern Garage opened their M1097R1 to find the fuel pump gone, the steering box removed, the power steering reservoir missing, and three steering box bolts loose on the frame after the ride from Fort Riley to Omaha [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:05:01]. Rasmussen Equipment says every Humvee they have picked up had the engine breather cut with a saw or grinder or smashed as part of demil, plus missing start, headlight, and blinker switches [B8X-aaJ2DpY @ 00:02:19]. The electrical system is a known quantity: 24 volts running off two 12-volt batteries. The Midnight Mechanic charged each battery separately on an old 12-volt charger, then wired positive to negative between them with the remaining posts to the truck, and warns to replace both as a pair [_tJQ6S_OaBc @ 00:05:02]. Midwestern Garage also found the gauge cluster pulled with nothing unhooked, and the batteries flat in their gigantic military-style 24-volt setup, yet the motor cranked over once a loose battery cable was tightened [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:09:29].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Spec selection comes first. Kevin24Seven's rule is to hunt for the 6.5-liter diesel with an automatic that shows park and overdrive; an M998 means the old 6.2 with three speeds, screaming at about 55 mph, while newer trucks like their own M1123 cruise at 60 to 65 [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:03:53]. In a later crash course they put it bluntly: get an A2 truck, not an A1, because overdrive lets you hit at least 80 and cruise at 65 [gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:01:09]. Midwestern Garage learned that lesson on an M1097R1 rebuilt in 2010 that still carries only the three-speed [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:00:44]. Topless trucks are the money play. A no-door, no-roof M1123 closed at about $11,600 while authentic hard-top, hard-door units run around $40,000; a brand-new surplus soft top kit was about $5,000 and an aftermarket hardtop roughly $7,000 to $8,000 [gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:02:34]. Ignore the odometer, because failed clusters get swapped and reset to zero. Read wear instead: steering wheel, turn signal stalk, start-stop switch paint, the shift label ink, and pedals polished by boots [gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:07:37]. Rock-chipped radiators and coolers signal high miles. The hard kill is blow-by at idle; Kevin24Seven flagged visible mist at the radiator cap as a probable junk motor some sucker would pay ten grand for [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:08:01].

Bidding runs on priority bids. You set a ceiling in advance and the system climbs in $100 increments until you lead or your max is beaten; it tells you when you are outbid but never by how much [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:04:37]. Kevin24Seven describes a mass wave of 50 to 100 Humvees closing on the same day, typically Wednesday, each lot open roughly five minutes, with priority bids exposing instantly so a truck can jump to about $12,000 at the bell [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:06:13]. Then come the 30-second overtimes, with no limit that they know of. In one account their first truck was 'won' around $8,000 and finished at $10,200; in another they thought they had it at $9,500 and only closed at $12,500 after repeated extensions [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:09:46]. Kevin24Seven expects the price to double or triple inside the window and would not go over $15,000 on any of them. Opening numbers look cheap: TK's Garage scrolled Marine Corps lots starting at $4,800, with open and hard-top trucks showing $7,000 and $6,000 [6iKYdGlqqP4 @ 00:07:29]. Split Builds adds that the start price is effectively the reserve, so you only bid against other people, and payment is due within three business days of winning [CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:01:30].

The invoice is where the bid becomes real. Kevin24Seven's $10,200 win printed at $12,290.40, built from a $1,030 transaction fee and a $50 SF-97 fee [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:09:22]. Rattlesnake Defense bid $4,400 on a 2008 M1097 R1 troop carrier and landed at about $5,500 in, plus another $600 to ship it from the Pennsylvania base [WzbjxUJRWKI @ 00:05:28]. For transport, Kevin24Seven was routed to the broker LTI Delivers, whose driver hauled the truck from Albany, Georgia to St. Louis for about $850, and they put the general range at $500 to $1,200 by distance [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:12:23]. Pickup itself is its own grind. Rasmussen Equipment, collecting at Yermo, California, reports the yard only loads until 2 p.m., only forklifts non-runners onto your trailer, and once left them waiting nearly two hours while a hand claimed no lunch break and then left for lunch [zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:00:49]. They also watched a forklift driver smash a Humvee's side and mirror while loading, so they now tell yard crews not to use a forklift unless they have to [zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:05:14]. They add there are no restrooms on site, and that a Facebook complaint page exists for loading damage, misrepresentations, and parts stolen off trucks [zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:05:27].

callout.title: Screening and wake-up tricks from buyers who have done it
callout.body: These are the field moves practitioners lean on to separate a good truck from a money pit and to get a dead one breathing.
items: Listen to the start clip: a healthy 6.5 fires on the first crank with a smooth idle; a hard start can be glow plugs or a start control box that runs almost $1,000 [Kevin24Seven — gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:09:53].

Buy topless: soft tops are usually junk, topless trucks go for a lot less once the auction starts, and brand-new tops in camo, black, white, or tan are on eBay [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:02:37].

Jump a listed non-runner with a slave cable from another 24-volt truck before tearing into it; Rasmussen Equipment fired a 'non-runner' M1097 R1 that only needed batteries [Rasmussen Equipment — zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:21:01].

Diagnose hard steering without a lift: if the brake pedal is equally hard running or off, it is a power steering issue because the pump also feeds the hydro-boost brakes [The Midnight Mechanic — _tJQ6S_OaBc @ 00:07:42].

sop_steps.title: Get cleared to bid
sop_steps.action: Create the GovPlanet account, request buying privileges, and put a credit card on file well before the target auction.
sop_steps.detail: Privileges can come within about 24 hours [Split Builds — CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:00:37], but account errors happen, so call the contact number and push through the hold queue [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:01:09].

sop_steps.title: Screen the listing like an inspector
sop_steps.action: Filter for 6.5 overdrive A2 trucks, then kill any listing with blow-by, hard starts, chipped coolers, or worn switches and pedals.
sop_steps.detail: Prioritize the 6.5 with park and overdrive and skip three-speed trucks [Kevin24Seven — gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:01:09]; treat visible blow-by at idle as a deal killer [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:07:18].

sop_steps.title: Priority-bid and ride the overtime
sop_steps.action: Set a priority bid at your true ceiling, be online at the close, and stay live through every 30-second extension.
sop_steps.detail: Overtimes keep reopening the lot and prices jump fast [Kevin24Seven — gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:06:28]; Kevin24Seven placed about $8,000 and would not go over $15,000 on any of these [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:08:50].

sop_steps.title: Pay, clear the EUC, and move the truck
sop_steps.action: Pay the invoice, submit the end-use certificate, then book pickup or a transport broker the moment it clears.
sop_steps.detail: Once the EUC clears you get seven days to collect before daily storage charges [Split Builds — CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:02:08]; budget $500 to $1,200 for transport depending on distance [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:12:23].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split runs through a single operator's own catalog. Kevin24Seven once steered every buyer toward GovPlanet, arguing private sellers price nine times out of ten higher and that mainstream resellers charge roughly double: a truck a buyer gets running and street legal for $20,000 themselves lists at $35,000 to $40,000 from a mainstream seller [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:14:50] [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:16:19]. By 2024 that same operator reported the Midwest Marketplace saturated with Humvees from flippers and burned-out owners whose wives want the oil-leaking truck out of the driveway, with Marketplace trucks clearing below current GovPlanet auctions by $2,000 to $3,000 or more, many already carrying street titles [TLQhxsY7JoE @ 00:04:26]. The private route buys a test drive, a gear-by-gear shift check, brake-pedal feel and an instant drive-home; the auction route buys end-use waiting of five to nine months, SF-97 chasing, $1,000 to $2,000 in fees and easily $1,000 in shipping. Kevin24Seven still leans toward doing it all themselves, admitting that instinct is probably to their own detriment. The updated verdict: steer the average buyer to Marketplace, keep GovPlanet for operators who want to do the wrenching and titling themselves, and accept that the old less-than-half-price advantage is gone in most states [TLQhxsY7JoE @ 00:12:49].

Operators read the same listings very differently. MotorTrend's Dirt Every Day host frames GovPlanet as semi sight unseen rather than blind: somebody has inspected every unit, non-runners are labeled as such, and runs-and-drives is stated in the description, with interior, exterior and under-hood photos instead of one blurry shot [Wg0ziRtQ9JM @ 00:01:41]. TK's Garage, normally a see-it-in-person buyer, said the drivetrain, suspension and joint photography was so detailed they could not see how a bidder would miss anything [6iKYdGlqqP4 @ 00:05:02]. Kevin24Seven counters that the yard only runs a limited function check, presumably starting the truck, cycling drive and reverse and confirming brakes, with no around-the-block test, because the contract is quantity over quality across thousands of units; a buyer who uncovers an undisclosed fault after signing is probably stuck with it [TLQhxsY7JoE @ 00:05:49]. Rasmussen Equipment, who hauls trucks out of the Yermo yard for buyers, goes further, pointing to a Facebook GovPlanet complaint page where buyers air misrepresentations and loading damage, and arguing Ritchie Bros has the money to deliver what buyers pay for without parts walking off or trucks getting busted up [zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:05:44]. Treat the photo set as evidence, the condition notes as a floor, and assume more is wrong than listed.

Spec doctrine also splits by mission. Kevin24Seven calls the 6.5-liter with park and overdrive the most important things on the listing, because a 6.2 three-speed tops out around 55 mph with the motor screaming, while an A2 overdrive truck hits 80 and cruises 65 [gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:00:49]. Rattlesnake Defense won a three-speed 2008 M1097R1 troop carrier at $4,400 with weak oil pressure and some blow-by and is happy with it, because it is a property truck that will be lucky to see 35 mph on dirt roads and does not care about briers, brush or scratches [WzbjxUJRWKI @ 00:07:15]. Midwestern Garage deliberately bought a non-running three-speed heavy-variant M1097R1 to drop in a 24-valve Cummins and a five-speed with a manual transfer case, planning taller tires in the meantime to claw back highway speed, treating the factory drivetrain as optional [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:07:41]. Kevin24Seven, who wanted one of the newer turbo trucks with air conditioning, put a $15,000 priority bid on one and lost when it closed near $20,000, then fell back to plans for an M1123 with air conditioning and turbo added later [5QTEGYGbQsw @ 00:00:21]. The playbook follows the use case: a highway daily driver, a dirt-road workhorse, or a swap platform each justify a different bid sheet.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is believing the clock. Kevin24Seven thought they had won at about $9,500, then watched repeated 30-second extensions push the hammer to $12,500, and on another truck a quote-unquote win at $8,000 ran to $10,200 through overtime after overtime, with no known cap on how many extensions fire [F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:09:46] [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:07:32]. Priority bids are exposed the moment the roughly five-minute window opens, so a listing can jump to about $12,000 almost instantly and then climb again. The second trap is heart-bidding. Reviewing a January 12 round, Kevin24Seven found a 2008 M1123 sold at $50,000, then a $45,000 hard-top turbo truck whose own listing showed lights not all working and visible blow-by, plus a string of soft-top trucks at $33,000 to $39,000 [5QTEGYGbQsw @ 00:01:37] [5QTEGYGbQsw @ 00:05:49]. Their read: these trucks are worth about $15,000 because they will need work, $25,000 to $30,000 is the personal ceiling even with money to blow, and $50,000 buys a Bronco Badlands that is more capable off-road and reliable on road trips. Set the ceiling before the window opens; Kevin24Seven's own rule was never over $15,000, and they still had to fight to $12,500 for a near-new truck.

Delivered trucks routinely hide work the listing never mentioned. Midnight Machine Shop's 2003 truck arrived with radio cables hacked off and a bundle of cut wiring through the floor, coolant overflow lines cut when the radiator was pulled, the fan-clutch quick connect left open so turning the wheel pumped power-steering fluid straight out, and an injection pump that appeared stuck after years sitting in a field [oACqhA0f4EM @ 00:07:08]. Midwestern Garage's listing said the brakes were inoperable with the master cylinder removed; in reality the brakes held pressure, but there was no steering box, no power-steering reservoir and no fuel pump [3QWRjujnz2E @ 00:02:04]. The Midnight Mechanic's 2002 truck ran but would not steer; the hydro-boost brake test pointed to a power-steering leak, and after bleeding by turning lock to lock about 40 times it still stalled at stop signs unless the throttle was feathered [_tJQ6S_OaBc @ 00:07:02]. Rasmussen Equipment's accidental-buy M1114 showed up with a destroyed engine breather, missing start and headlight switches, saltwater rust through the slant back, and a fluid leak from the coolers that kept it stuck on the trailer [B8X-aaJ2DpY @ 00:10:04]. Budget for the missing parts, not the photographed ones.

The paperwork and the yard bleed time and money even on clean trucks. Split Builds paid within three business days, then waited the full 12 weeks for end-use clearance from October to January, with only seven days after clearance to collect before a daily storage rate kicks in [CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:02:08]. Kevin24Seven tallied a roughly $10,200 win at $12,290.40 once a $1,030 transaction fee and a $50 SF-97 fee landed, then added about $1,000 to ship from Georgia to Missouri [gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:09:22]. At pickup, Rasmussen Equipment waited nearly two hours in the Yermo desert after a yard hand claimed no lunch break and then left for lunch, and on an earlier visit watched a forklift operator smash the side and mirror of another buyer's Humvee and bounce it on the forks onto a transport trailer; their standing rule is to tell the yard not to use a forklift unless it has to [zqnmA4kt0RU @ 00:05:14]. Titling can stall after delivery: Rattlesnake Defense's West Virginia DMV rejected the notarized form as not a certificate, and nobody would accept the six-digit serial as a VIN for insurance [WzbjxUJRWKI @ 00:07:32]. Map the title route in your state before the hammer drops.

callout.title: Clear These Four Traps Before Any Bid Goes Live
callout.body: Every item below was hit firsthand by a practitioner who bought, hauled, or wrenched on a GovPlanet Humvee. Run the list before the five-minute window opens.
items: Kill any listing showing blow-by mist from the radiator cap at idle; a healthy truck costs no more at auction [Kevin24Seven — gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:04:18]
Write the walk-away number down before bidding, because 30-second overtime extensions keep firing after you think you have won [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:09:46]
Plan for up to 12 weeks of end-use clearance and a seven-day pickup window before daily storage charges start [Split Builds — CkfJvTDwa2w @ 00:02:08]
Confirm your DMV will accept the paperwork and that an insurer will take the six-digit serial before you win [Rattlesnake Defense — WzbjxUJRWKI @ 00:07:32]

action_checklist: Create the GovPlanet account, request bidding approval, and call customer service directly when the approval process glitches, expecting long hold times [Kevin24Seven — F0AkAibFp2g @ 00:00:49]
Filter listings for the 6.5-liter diesel with park and overdrive so the truck cruises at 65 instead of screaming at 55 [Kevin24Seven — gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:00:49]
Ignore the odometer and audit wear on the steering wheel, switch paint, shifter label, pedals and radiator chips in the listing photos [Kevin24Seven — gtS8l93r5cw @ 00:05:45]
Purchase the clean SF-97 during checkout, since it is the lifeline for making the truck street legal later [Kevin24Seven — gXjTPh7cGHU @ 00:08:07]

chapters.question_prompt: Once I win a vehicle, what titles, registration steps, and repair costs do I face to make it street legal and worth the money?
chapters.title: Titles, Street-Legal Registration, and True Build Cost
chapters.subtitle: SF-97 and MCO paperwork, bill-of-sale-only items, salvage-title registration, Humvee street-legal steps and total build costs, buying without a dealer license, Copart mistakes, and post-purchase GovDeals F-150 and Escape verdicts
chapters.executive_summary: Operators buying government surplus agree that paperwork decides value. Kevin24Seven and Dirt Legal treat the SF-97 as the key to a clean title on GovPlanet Humvees. End-user approval runs 3-5 months and the SF-97 another 4-5. Zero Tax Tags and Wisdom & Authority Title Solutions warn that a bill of sale alone transfers nothing, and that a missing MCO usually means no title record. The street numbers are blunt. A $12,500 Humvee hit $14,800 after shipping and tax, $17,777 bare-bones, and $35,547 fully built. A basic four-man build pencils out at $21,335. Fees run 7-12% on GovDeals, 8% at Flying Wheels' New Hampshire auction, and 0% on GSA fleet sales. The disagreements are about three things: Missouri plate-versus-title sequencing, paid title services versus DIY, and whether New Hampshire's bill-of-sale registration travels to other states.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who has handled titled surplus treats the paperwork chain as the real asset. The steel comes second. Zero Tax Tags draws the hard line: the title is the deed, registration is renewable permission to drive, and a bill of sale is only a receipt. Ownership takes the signed title plus the bill of sale [uOA3FOVLCGA @ 00:01:35]. The same channel flags that government does not title its own vehicles. The SF-97 therefore has to carry reassignment forms across the full chain of custody, and some states add military-specific rules [uOA3FOVLCGA @ 00:03:13]. Wisdom & Authority Title Solutions backs this up from the manufacturer side. The MCO starts the title trail, and the title carries it across state lines, such as Pennsylvania to West Virginia. When there is no MCO, there is no title record nine times out of ten, and the DMV may have to generate a VIN [-S82T9iXF7Q @ 00:06:31]. Dirt Legal puts dollar figures on the military version of that chain. The buyer signs an end-user agreement barring overseas export, then pays $25 for the bill of sale and $50 for the SF-97. A clean title arrives in up to eight weeks, and the whole GovPlanet process runs up to six months [9EAPaeoXhFs @ 00:01:46].

The second point of agreement is to price every lot as if it is broken, because listings routinely miss defects. Flying Wheels works a public New Hampshire surplus auction on that premise. Everything sells as-is, so preview the day before and bid assuming the item does not run. Know your market, set limits ahead of time, and add 10% to cover the 8% premium [SEESfrbGoLY @ 00:19:19]. FlatBroke Garage reports roughly 80% winners across nine or ten GovDeals vehicles. The advice there is to call the town or village, set an inspection date, and fire the vehicles up in person. Yet the F-150 went uninspected on a minimum bid, and the same operator steers clear of drug and police seizure units entirely [pN1E-KA7qxw @ 00:04:50]. Kevin24Seven learned what trusting listing copy costs. A GovPlanet Humvee advertised with only a weak brake pedal turned out to be described incorrectly [Vl0TRUioSn0 @ 00:01:15]. The basic build budget now carries $2,500 for repairs, because even trucks listed as perfect need work. The TCM and the start box are singled out as the expensive failure points [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:16:39]. Nobody in this group bids on the seller's description alone.

The third point of agreement is that the hammer price is the smallest number in the deal. Vantor Insider frames landed cost as a 5-12% buyer fee plus sales tax. Payment goes by wire within 48 hours, and removal is due within 5-7 business days, so the cash and the transport have to be lined up before the bid lands [tBIT1SUqIz8 @ 00:18:14]. Kevin24Seven shows it on a single Humvee. A $12,500 winning bid picked up $800 in shipping from Georgia to St. Louis and roughly $1,500 in registration and taxes. That made $14,800 before a wrench turned [Vl0TRUioSn0 @ 00:01:54]. FlatBroke Garage shows the same math at the cheap end: a $2,600 F-150 took a 12% auction fee of about $300 and landed near $2,900 all-in [pN1E-KA7qxw @ 00:35:03]. AutoHacker claims 15 years and more than 12,000 cars bought for clients, and posts the most brutal ratio. A Hawaii car bought for $1,450 cost about $3,700 and five weeks just to ship [wNIgM_BLGik @ 00:09:33]. Every operator here budgets fees, tax, freight, and title paperwork before setting a ceiling. Any number that skips those lines is a fantasy price, and the overrun lands on the buyer.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Kevin24Seven's GovPlanet run is the most complete buy-side playbook. On price, a Humvee showing $4,800 will clear at least $6,000-7,000. The live close runs about 15 minutes, with a 30-second extension after every bid. A $7,000 bid that looked like a win ended at $12,000, against a pre-set $15,000 walk-away [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:21:20]. Waldo's World shows how that extension clock can work in a patient buyer's favor. Lots ran online in batches five minutes apart, and a rival's last-second bids kept stretching the Marine lot by at least two minutes each time. The two lots ended up overlapping, and a low bid on the Army truck went uncontested, buying it sight unseen [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:54:25]. After the win, Kevin24Seven says to expect three to five months for EUC approval. There are no storage fees during that wait, and about two weeks to collect once approval lands [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:25:16]. Transport went through VeriTread with LTI for about $800, roughly $150 more than self-pickup, and the operator advises budgeting a flat $1,000 [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:26:01]. The SF-97 then took another four to five months to arrive, so the money stays parked for most of a year before the truck sees pavement.

Kevin24Seven reports titling in Missouri without a middleman and without mods. First, buy a DOR 551 at the DMV for about $30. Then take it, the SF-97, and the truck to a Troop C highway patrol inspection station, by appointment only [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:29:40]. The companion video compresses the same route into three moves. Get the DOR 551, which the operator compares to titling a dune buggy. Wait out the SF-97, the paper that shows the truck was not stolen: about three months to clear for pickup, then two to three more for the form. Then present everything at highway patrol, walk out with a street VIN and a title, and apply for plates. If one DMV stonewalls, try another, because all DMVs are not created equal [VvAg_yxxkPo @ 00:01:58]. Insurance came through State Farm at roughly $30 a month after Progressive failed, with the advice to move straight to the next carrier. Missouri also runs no diesel emissions test [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:32:00]. Waldo's World reports a lighter path for the bill-of-sale crowd: New Hampshire registration needs only a bill of sale, while other states vary [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:53:21]. The playbook is to call the state first and match the paperwork to the counter.

The build sheets show where the true cost lands. Kevin24Seven's basic four-man build starts at $11,000 for the truck including fees, then adds:
- $675 for five run-flat inserts at $135 each
- $4,500 for a NOS four-man soft-top kit with doors from eBay
- $200 for fiberglass repair
- $350 for gauges
- $510 for rear seats and supports
- $800 for Dirt Legal titling
- $300 for rear belts and brackets
- $2,500 for repairs
- $500 for a spare
The total comes to $21,335 [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:19:39]. The earlier hardtop truck ran $2,977.30 in maintenance alone, led by a $937 start box and a $552 steering box [Vl0TRUioSn0 @ 00:04:08]. Upgrades then stacked on top: a $1,995 top, $3,575 hard doors, $2,422 for five tires, $2,394 rock rails, a $1,077 winch, and a $600 tire carrier the operator would not really recommend. That pushed the full build to $35,547, against a bare-bones $17,777 [Vl0TRUioSn0 @ 00:09:22]. Waldo's World prices the parts that sink a cheap non-runner: about $4,000 for a set of four doors, $800 per tire on 16.5-inch rims, and roughly $2,500 for an alternator, with used parts on eBay as the main source [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:53:56]. Doors, tires, and electrical boxes decide whether a bargain stays a bargain.

callout.title: Screening tricks operators use before the bid
callout.body: These are the filters and diagnostics practitioners run to separate a cheap truck from an expensive one before money moves.
items: Filter GovPlanet sold listings for two-door units with soft top and truck body, because two-doors go for far less, and target M1123s; newer units cost more [Kevin24Seven — d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:02:24]

Run the idle-hour math: one idle hour equals about 33 miles of wear, so 55,000 miles with 6,500 hours reads like about 214,000 miles, while 1,700 hours means an engine barely broken in [Vantor Insider — tBIT1SUqIz8 @ 00:08:24]

A healthy Humvee fires on the first crank. Hard starting points to glow plugs first, then the injection or lift pump, then a worn motor. Stay away from visible blow-by unless you are prepared to rebuild a motor [Kevin24Seven — k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:14:47]

Carfax does not cover salvage, so pull autostat or Vindoctor at $7.99 on NMVTIS data, and skip certificate of destruction and non-repairable titles, which cannot be registered [AutoHacker — wNIgM_BLGik @ 00:03:20]

sop_steps.title: Confirm pickup access before bidding
sop_steps.action: Open a free GovPlanet account and call customer service to confirm the pickup site is open.
sop_steps.detail: EUC and title documents can be delayed, and only certain sites, Pennsylvania and Nevada at the time, were open for pickup. Expect long holds, though service is pretty good once you get through [Kevin24Seven — k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:02:10]

sop_steps.title: Set the ceiling with fees baked in
sop_steps.action: Fix a walk-away number that already includes the buyer's premium, then stop bidding at it.
sop_steps.detail: Know your market, set limits ahead of time, and add 10% for the premium. Kevin24Seven held a $15,000 walk-away and closed at $12,000 after 30-second extensions [Flying Wheels — SEESfrbGoLY @ 00:19:19]

sop_steps.title: Wait out EUC and the SF-97
sop_steps.action: Do not try to title the truck until the SF-97 is in hand.
sop_steps.detail: Clearance for pickup took about 3 months, then another 2-3 months for the SF-97, which proves the truck was not stolen [Kevin24Seven — VvAg_yxxkPo @ 00:01:21]

sop_steps.title: Inspect, title, plate, insure
sop_steps.action: Take the DOR 551, SF-97, and truck to Troop C, then get plates and shop insurers.
sop_steps.detail: Buy the DOR 551 for about $30, book the Troop C inspection by appointment, then take the street VIN and title to the DMV. State Farm wrote coverage at about $30/month after Progressive failed [Kevin24Seven — k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:29:40]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a surplus Humvee needs a paid titling service at all. Kevin24Seven insists he made his GovPlanet truck street legal himself with 'no middleman' and no modifications, and he argues other channels overcomplicate the job: red states are easy, and for blue states his answer is to 'just get a prius' [VvAg_yxxkPo @ 00:03:12]. Dirt Legal runs the opposite playbook, warning that private-party trucks need a theft check because there have been base thefts, and that some states will not title a Humvee at all, which is exactly the gap their paid service fills [9EAPaeoXhFs @ 00:02:19]. The contradiction sits inside Kevin24Seven's own catalog: in his basic-build breakdown he calls Dirt Legal 'the best and easiest' option, discloses that they sponsor him, and books an $800 line item for the service inside a $21,335 budget [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:14:13]. Waldo's World adds a third data point from New Hampshire, where registering his truck needed only a bill of sale, while conceding that other states vary [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:53:21]. The operator read is simple: your state, not the auction house, decides whether the DIY highway-patrol route, a bill-of-sale registration, or a paid out-of-state service is the cheapest path to plates.

Humvee selection splits Kevin24Seven against himself. In his full buying walkthrough he tells bidders to avoid soft-top units because they sell for $5,000 to $10,000 more and the tops are usually shot, notes hardtops can climb to $15,000 to $20,000, and reports paying $12,000 for his [k5WD_GKlQhs @ 00:03:11]. In his basic-build video he flips the filter, hunting sold listings for two-door soft-top and truck-body units because two-doors 'go for far less' [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:02:24], and he rates a $9,500 runner with hard steering, minor blow-by, and oil and fuel leaks as a 'really good deal' [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:04:30]. Waldo's World played a completely different game: he bought two non-running trucks sight unseen at an online-only government auction, paying $3,600 for an Army M1097 and about $4,500 for a Marine M1123 on a day when running Humvees went for roughly $10,000 [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:55:41]. That discount came with a long wrench bill, including an in-frame bearing job and a lift-pump and check-valve chase. The trade-off is clear: Kevin24Seven pays for a running platform and budgets repairs on top, while Waldo's World buys dead iron cheap, harvests one truck to revive the other, and estimates another $5,000 just to complete the second unit.

On civilian vehicles the split is inspection discipline and broker use. FlatBroke Garage, with nine or ten GovDeals vehicles and about 80% winners, admits he skipped the scheduled inspection on his F-150 and simply placed a minimum bid, even though buyers can contact the town, set an inspection date, and fire the vehicles up [pN1E-KA7qxw @ 00:04:50]. We Hustle Daily takes the hard line on Copart: inspect in person, because buyers who purchase out of state 'are some Maniacs' [VRmsT2o_6og @ 00:06:29]. Brokers split the field again. Vantor Insider calls the dealer-license requirement a myth for government surplus and warns that salvage brokers charge unlicensed buyers $400 to $1,200, with $800 in broker fees typically buying a branded title [tBIT1SUqIz8 @ 00:05:30]. AutoHacker argues the opposite math on salvage pools, showing a $15,000 bid costs $2,250 in public fees versus $650 through a broker, and $750 versus $525 on a $5,000 bid [wNIgM_BLGik @ 00:08:02]. The workable split: go direct on GovDeals, GSA, and municipal surplus where the public bids openly, and only pay a broker on Copart or IAAI when the fee spread favors the broker and the title is clean enough to register.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive surprise is a listing that lies by omission. Kevin24Seven won his GovPlanet Humvee at $12,500 on a description claiming only a weak brake pedal, which 'turned out to be incorrect' [Vl0TRUioSn0 @ 00:01:15]; his maintenance tally reached $2,977.30, led by a $937 start box and a $552 steering box. In his basic-build budget he books a flat $2,500 repair reserve because 'even trucks listed as perfect' fail at the expensive points, naming the TCM and the start box [d2qrhLbKEbI @ 00:16:39]. Waldo's World hit the same wall on his non-runners: he moved the ignition switch and protective control box from the Marine truck into the Army truck and warned that these boxes commonly don't work [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:02:02]. His fuel-system chase found sediment in the filter, two bad lift pumps, and a stuck check valve; he called the just-under-$300 milspec valve 'ridiculous,' swapped in a roughly $20 substitute, and cracked it by overtightening [UhFstJrc_44 @ 00:32:14]. The pattern across both builders is that the cheap hammer price is only the entry ticket: start boxes, steering boxes, lift pumps, and valves are the line items that turn a bargain into a bill, so the repair reserve has to be in the bid ceiling before the auction clock starts.

Civilian salvage and surplus lots carry their own traps. FlatBroke Garage's F-150 came with diesel-contaminated fuel, broken 4x4 vacuum lines, a stripped drain plug, and a bad ABS module, and he warns that pressure-washing ruined a coil pack [pN1E-KA7qxw @ 00:24:20]. We Hustle Daily flags Copart storage fees that kick in after three days and escalate in $5 steps, $5, $10, $15, and says they are mandatory or you lose buying access [VRmsT2o_6og @ 00:07:59]. AutoHacker, citing 15 years and more than 12,000 cars bought for clients, documents staged cars: a Lexus that sold for $8,600 on February 23, 2022 later resold for $20,000, so he says treat those as parts cars [wNIgM_BLGik @ 00:02:43]. He also warns that certificate-of-destruction and non-repairable titles cannot be registered at all, which turns a cheap win into a parts-only asset [wNIgM_BLGik @ 00:04:53]. Logistics compound the damage: his Hawaii example cost about $3,700 and five weeks to ship against a $1,450 purchase price. The economics check is to price the title brand, the storage clock, and transport before bidding, because any one of them can erase the spread on a car that looked like a steal on the lot photos.

Paperwork is where surplus buyers get stranded after paying. Kevin24Seven got plates before his title by using the manufacturer number from the SF97, then received a state letter demanding a Troop C inspection and a DOR 551, 'probably because i have a short vin,' and admits he is unsure whether his plates are valid [VvAg_yxxkPo @ 00:04:06]. Zero Tax Tags warns that a bill of sale is only a receipt and 'does not transfer ownership by itself'; ownership takes the signed title plus the bill of sale, and an SF-97 needs reassignment forms covering the full chain of custody [uOA3FOVLCGA @ 00:01:35]. Wisdom & Authority Title Solutions adds that a missing MCO means no title record 'nine times out of 10,' and the DMV may have to generate a VIN [-S82T9iXF7Q @ 00:06:31]. chapters.question_prompt: How does military surplus reach public auction, and which scrap-coded lots are traps versus genuine bargains?
chapters.title: Military Disposition, Scrap Codes, and Diesel Generators
chapters.subtitle: DLA Disposition Services reverse logistics, agency disposal-code scrap traps, zero-hour trucks and generators sold as unserviceable, home-size surplus diesels, the hammer-to-service cost gap, CMP surplus rifles, and military surplus pallet sorting
chapters.executive_summary: DLA Disposition Services feeds public sales only after DoD reutilization, federal transfer and donation screening. Practitioners agree that the condition codes stamped on what reaches the block describe paperwork, not wear. Vantor Surplus documents condemned Tactical Quiet Generators showing 0.8 to 2.4 hours after COSIS inspection clocks expired, plus zero-hour trucks dumped as scrap under pure-fleet purges. Engine Auction tracks MEP-803A, Onan, WhisperWatt and Kohler diesels hammering between $890 and $1,350, each revived with a $15 to $22 fix, and prices a home install at $1,560 all-in. Vantor Insider counters that landed cost averages 42% above hammer price. The same channel flags demil codes D and F, missing SF97 titles, cannibalized fence queens and hazmat removal riders as traps. Gear Rack shows the soft-goods side: sort, wash, photograph and list pallet lots piece by piece.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The Defense Logistics Agency's own staff lay out the pipeline every surplus buyer sits downstream of: property lands at more than 100 disposal sites across four continents, gets offered first for reutilization inside the Department of Defense, then transferred to other federal agencies or donated to state and local governments, and only what survives that screening is made available to the public through the DoD surplus property sales program [8HnHBuGYT6Y @ 00:01:48]. At Fort Meade, the team describes roughly 6,000 pieces of property ranging from pistols and pens to aircraft parts, boilers, stoves and gym equipment, all flipped into programs like computers for learning, transfer, donation and foreign military sales before anything reaches a bidder [HYKDZ7wW8ik @ 00:00:40]. Vantor Surplus argues the word unserviceable on that stream is an accounting label, not a diagnosis. A two-letter supply condition code on Department of Defense form 1348-1A, most often F for unserviceable repairable or H for unserviceable condemned scrap, scares off amateurs who picture a seized crankshaft, yet condemned MEP-803A and MEP-806B units open up with 0.8 to 2.4 hours on the analog meter, untouched cylinder crosshatching and acoustic foam that has never seen soot [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:04:09]. The shared premise is blunt: the label describes the paperwork trail, and the buyer has to go inspect the iron.

Four separate speakers converge on the same force driving clean equipment onto the block: calendars and budgets, not wear. Vantor Surplus traces the generator flood to the COSIS rule that stored units get a load-bank inspection every 24 to 36 months. Once the Tactical Quiet Generator line lost its sustainment budget to the AMMPS program, the 36-month clock expired, the database stripped condition code A, and a disposal clerk clearing 40,000 square feet reclassified 200 unissued skids to F or H because nobody signs an engineering release without funding [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:13:44]. On the truck side, the same channel describes a pure fleet standardization mandate that deactivates a legacy national stock number, cuts the Defense Working Capital Fund storage subsidy, and pushes property officers to downgrade zero-hour rigs to scrap classification S rather than sit through a 14-month interagency screening period [xwqMdeMDNSg @ 00:05:34]. Engine Auction reports the civilian mirror image: FEMA Assistance to Firefighters Grant money only buys new generators that talk Modbus to digital transfer switches, NFPA 110 drives 10-year replacement on life-safety units, and municipal statutes forbid keeping the redundant asset, so a 98.4-hour Onan hit GovDeals [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:05:00]. State highway departments retire pre-Tier 4 WhisperWatts once DERA grant terms and zero book depreciation line up [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:18:17].

The second consensus point is that the hammer price is never the bill. Vantor Insider puts the average gap between winning bid and in-service cost at 42%, and says experienced liquidators calculate landed price first by stacking buyer premiums, dock rigging tariffs, compliance holds and the mechanical reset required after government storage [WGe7vjs5ktc @ 00:00:16]. Vantor Surplus lists the same stack on a $1,500 tactical truck: buyer premiums that often exceed 10 to 18% of the final bid, instant state sales tax, and daily storage penalties if the iron is not removed within 10 working days [VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:04:13]. CabinDad, who bought two mobile kitchens off GovPlanet to run an off-grid property in the middle of a national forest, tells buyers to sort every site by their own state because otherwise they are paying shipping, which they call not as straightforward as you think but also not that hard [aH3cAZ1RXvE @ 00:01:27]. The Vantor Insider veteran's 30-year verdict ties it together: stop looking at how cheap the current bid is and start calculating why the fleet manager refused to fix it, because a legitimate bargain leaves verifiable proof of health in its condition code, frame rail seams, engine hour-to-mile ratio, dry copper connector pins and clean environmental release sheet [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:15:42].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Lot decoding comes before the bid button. The Vantor Insider veteran reads the demilitarization letter first: code A requires no mutilation, code Q with integrity code six allows conditional civilian road use, code D mandates total destruction by melting, cutting or deforming before title passes, and code F requires government-verified demil cutting. Even a truck that escapes the torch stays a driveway ornament without an original standard form 97, since 42 state motor vehicle departments refuse highway registration without it [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:02:26]. On generators, Vantor Surplus says one digit changes everything: a zero in the middle of the MEP model code, as in 803, 805 or 806, means 50 or 60 hertz utility power, while a one, as in 813, 815 or 816, means a 400 hertz aviation and radar unit that will overheat and burn out standard 60 hertz induction motors [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:16:44]. The closing rule from that channel is to verify the middle digit and check the analog hour counter against the preservation tag before placing an offer [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:20:09]. For trucks, the same operators ignore the cab odometer, wipe preservative grease off the riveted 3-inch brass depot rebuild plate, and look for RAA, CAAA or ANAD stamped alongside STD for standard bores and crankshaft journals [xwqMdeMDNSg @ 00:15:06].

The money is made in the gap between the clerk's fault note and the actual fault. Engine Auction tracked an MEP-803A with 410 hours that hammered for $1,080 on GovPlanet out of Red River Army Depot under condition code H, cranks but will not start. The real culprit was a stuck Facet cube lift pump that never built 5 PSI, leaving low-fuel-pressure switch S14 open; the fix was a $16 Posi-Flo pump, a 7/16 wrench and a 30-second prime [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:08:35]. A Corps of Engineers MEP-803A that ran smoothly but showed no AC voltage sold for $1,120 because silver sulfide tarnish on reconnection switch S2 blocked the field flashing current and popped breaker CB2. A $15 can of DeoxIT D5, ten handle cycles and a two-second flash swung the needle to 240 volts and 60.0 Hz [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:10:40]. A fire-station Onan that shut down after 15 seconds turned out to be an air pocket around the low-coolant probe, cleared in 4 minutes with a $22 jug of coolant [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:06:31]. Vantor Surplus adds that a warehouse unit spinning 1,800 RPM with zero volts has usually just lost residual magnetism, restored by touching 12-volt jumper leads across the exciter field terminals for 2 seconds while the engine runs [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:18:37].

Engine Auction ran the residential math line by line: a $1,100 winning bid plus a 10% buyer premium of $110, $140 in parts for a breaker interlock kit, 50-amp weatherproof inlet box and double-pole breaker, and $210 for 30 feet of 6-gauge four-conductor SOOW cord with twist-lock ends comes to $1,560 all-in. That stands against a $21,000 turnkey dealer quote for a 22 kW air-cooled standby unit, a claimed saving of $19,440 [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:27:03]. The same channel notes GSA Auctions charges a 0% buyer's premium while GovDeals and Municibid fire districts add 5 to 12.5%, so the bid cap sits 10% below target budget and the Q&A tab gets used to confirm station forklift loading and whether the maintenance logbook is included [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:17:23]. Soft-goods resellers run a different machine entirely. Gear Rack broke down a semi-truck load of unsorted military surplus by grouping like items first, logging the piles on a spreadsheet, binning them on shelves so orders can be pulled, pre-washing used APFU, and setting aside never-photographed one-offs to shoot and list later [m4wTDvPYQuA @ 00:17:42]. They split the Air Warrior vest from its pouches because a buyer might want the blower pouch but not the vest, so pieces move faster sold separately [m4wTDvPYQuA @ 00:04:35].

callout.title: Pickup-Day Moves That Separate Mechanics From Scrap Bidders
callout.body: These are the field moves the practitioners use to turn a scrap-coded or non-running listing into a working machine without destroying it on the first crank.
items: Bar preserved engines over by hand first: put a 3/4-inch breaker bar on the front crankshaft damper bolt for two full revolutions, then work the manual primer for 5 minutes, because pooled preservative oil lets a 24-volt starter bend a forged rod on the first turn [Vantor Surplus — xwqMdeMDNSg @ 00:16:01]

Never hit a long-parked tactical diesel with aerosol starting fluid; drain the fuel cell and flush the lines before turning the key or risk cracked piston rings and bent connecting rods [Vantor Surplus — VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:13:00]

Fire-truck compartment generators that will not crank on a pallet are usually the NFPA 1901 parking-brake interlock: flip the internal toggle from remote to local or place a jumper between pin 4 of the J2 Deutsch connector and chassis ground [Engine Auction — TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:16:13]

Target faded DOT-orange WhisperWatts sitting on belly skids after the county pulled the trailer; casual bidders pass on a box without wheels, and an $80 battery wins a 61 dB diesel for $1,150 [Engine Auction — t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:18:57]

sop_steps.title: Source and Bid Across Portals
sop_steps.action: Register on GSA Auctions, GovDeals, Municibid and GovPlanet, filter by home state, and cap bids for premiums.
sop_steps.detail: Any citizen over 18 can register on GSA Auctions with a driver's license at a 0% buyer's premium, while fire districts on GovDeals and Municibid add 5 to 12.5%, so set the cap 10% under budget and use the Q&A tab to confirm forklift loading and logbook inclusion [Engine Auction — TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:17:23]; sort each site by state to avoid paying shipping [CabinDad — aH3cAZ1RXvE @ 00:01:27].

sop_steps.title: Decode the Lot Before Bidding
sop_steps.action: Read the demil code, condition code, MEP middle digit and hour meter against the preservation tag.
sop_steps.detail: Verify the middle digit on the data plate is a zero for 60 Hz output and check the analog hour counter against the preservation tag before placing an offer [Vantor Surplus — VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:20:09]; walk away from demil code D or F and confirm an original SF97 comes with any vehicle [Vantor Insider — vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:02:26].

sop_steps.title: Run the Driveway Commissioning Autopsy
sop_steps.action: Drain and inspect oil and filter, purge old fuel, install new filters and treat fuel.
sop_steps.detail: Slice open the old spin-on oil filter with tin snips to check for bronze flakes or steel shavings, refill with 15W40, then drain old fuel, install new primary and secondary filters, and add biocide plus 2 oz of Stanadyne or Opti-Lube lubricity additive to protect the rotary pump plungers [Engine Auction — t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:27:45].

sop_steps.title: Wire, Unbond Neutral and Burn Off Wet Stacking
sop_steps.action: Install an interlock or transfer switch with an inlet box, float the generator neutral, and load-test hot.
sop_steps.detail: Never backfeed with a double male cord; use a UL 1008 transfer switch or interlock kit with a hold-down screw, unbolt the L0-to-frame neutral strap and verify infinite resistance [Engine Auction — TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:19:24]; set no-load frequency to 60.3 Hz, then run at 70% load for an hour until exhaust passes 550 degrees Fahrenheit to clear carbon off the injector tips [Engine Auction — t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:29:35].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in military disposition is over what a scrap stencil actually tells you. Vantor Insider treats the code as a verdict: the unit already failed an internal maintenance audit, so the discipline is to 'stop looking at how cheap the current bid is and start calculating why the fleet manager refused to fix it' [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:15:42]. Vantor Surplus argues the opposite for diesel generators, reporting that clerks reclassify expired, unfunded depot stock into condition code F or H, so unserviceable means 'an expired calendar date on an unfunded spreadsheet,' not broken metal [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:14:58]. The channel's truck episode pushes further, describing property officers downgrading zero-hour rigs to scrap classification S so commercial dealerships never see the lot and only regional shredders bid by the pound [xwqMdeMDNSg @ 00:05:50]. Engine Auction sits between the camps with a concrete lot: an MEP 803A tagged condition code H, 'cranks but will not start,' hammered at $1,080, and the fault traced to a stuck lift pump that a $16 replacement cured [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:07:51]. The code opens the investigation rather than closing it. One camp reads the tag as hidden liability; the other reads it as an accounting artifact you diagnose on the ramp before the paddle goes up.

Practitioners also clash on what a 10 kW generator really costs once the gavel drops. Vantor Insider puts an average 42% gap between hammer and in-service spend and prices the MEP 803A at $3,600 hammer versus $7,400 landed, blaming an end use certificate, a 6-week trade security wait, carrier scheduling fees and hardened fluorosilicone fuel o-rings [WGe7vjs5ktc @ 00:07:32]. Engine Auction runs a far leaner sheet: $1,100 winning bid, a 10% premium of $110, $140 in interlock and inlet parts and $210 of 6-gauge SOOW cord, for $1,560 all-in against a $21,000 dealer standby quote [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:27:03]. Fee assumptions diverge as well. Vantor Surplus warns platform premiums often exceed 10 to 18% of the final bid and insists the hammer price is never the final invoice [VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:03:56]. Engine Auction's fire-station playbook counters that GSA Auctions charges a 0% premium and the depot forklift loads your trailer free on a standard form 114 receipt, while fire-district lots on GovDeals and Municibid carry 5 to 12.5% [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:17:23]. Venue choice and paperwork exposure swing the math more than the hammer, so the same nameplate can become a $1,560 home plant or a $7,400 project.

Sourcing playbooks split along buyer type. CabinDad works the portals in parallel, watching every site constantly, using GovPlanet for larger equipment and bulk boots and clothing while GSA Auctions and GovDeals add local government lots on top of federal stock, then sorting by state to avoid paying shipping [aH3cAZ1RXvE @ 00:01:10]. The Rental Journey skips most bidding entirely, walking an unadvertised provincial surplus warehouse where chairs run 15 dollars, most stock sells outright, and buying 20 or 30 of an item earns a deal [utk0mvTVyMM @ 00:03:11]. Gear Rack plays volume at the other extreme, taking a semi-truck load of unsorted military surplus, sorting by item and size, and debating whether to keep complete air crew vests intact before deciding to split the pouches because 'it's more likely to sell separate' [m4wTDvPYQuA @ 00:04:35]. Survival Gear makes the case for buying direct from the government source rather than the flipper: CMP rack grade Garands run under $500 while resellers ask $1,000 to $1,500 [ZSzUyNfsBZ0 @ 00:04:34]. The contrast is about leverage. Portal sniping rewards patience and state filters, walk-in surplus rewards bulk relationships and fast repeat visits, and pallet sorting rewards raw labor plus item-level listing discipline.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The generator traps are electrical, and they bite after the win. Vantor Surplus flags the middle digit: MEP 813, 815 and 816 units share the housing and engine of the 803, 805 and 806, but a one in that slot means 400 hertz aviation and radar power that cannot run 60 hertz induction motors, compressors or transformers without overheating the windings [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:17:06]. The same channel reports zero-hour units spinning a clean 1,800 RPM while the voltmeter reads zero because exciter magnetism decayed in storage; a two-second 12-volt flash across the field terminals restores regulation [VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:18:53]. Engine Auction's commissioning guide warns that most military and municipal generators ship with the neutral bus bonded to the frame, which must be unbonded so the house panel remains the single bonding point [t9kRwYmHNpE @ 00:28:29]. Its fire-station playbook names the worst shortcut outright: a double male cord into a dryer outlet 'backfeeds 7,200 volts onto down street lines,' so the hookup goes through a UL 1008 listed manual transfer switch or a mechanical interlock kit instead [TCWzENE_0pw @ 00:18:30]. Each failure looks like a dead or dangerous machine on day one, yet traces back to a configuration choice the buyer either made or inherited.

Rolling-stock failures are mostly paperwork and startup physics. Vantor Insider describes bidders pushing a $500 opener to $4,500 on an intact six-wheel drive truck, then learning that code D mandates total destruction, code F requires cutting under government verification, and that without an original standard form 97 issued at sale, 42 state motor vehicle departments refuse highway registration [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:03:00]. Vantor Surplus adds the waiting game: the end use certificate triggers a background check lasting 3 weeks to several months while the purchased machine sits outdoors in rain and forklift traffic [VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:04:54]. Startup is the next kill zone. On depot-preserved trucks, 2 ounces of grade 30 preservative oil can pool on a piston crown and let a 24-volt starter bend a forged connecting rod on the very first revolution, so the engine gets barred over two full turns by hand with a breaker bar on the damper bolt [xwqMdeMDNSg @ 00:16:01]. On long-parked haulers, civilians who reach for aerosol starting fluid crack piston rings or bend rods; seasoned mechanics drain the fuel cell and flush the lines before the key ever turns [VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:13:00]. Skipping any of these converts a cheap hammer into a parked liability.

Economics checks come down to reading what the listing hides. Vantor Insider's hour-meter rule converts every idle or PTO hour into 33 highway miles, so a 49,000-mile utility pickup showing 6,900 hours has endured 227,700 miles of internal friction, which makes the odometer the wrong gauge to bid against [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:06:06]. The same yard veteran calls the hazmat lot the deadliest: a $100 win on a transformer or shelter transfers environmental custody at award, and if PCBs exceed 50 parts per million or friable asbestos is present, a default lets the agency bill $9,000 to $18,000 in remediation straight to the winner [vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:15:21]. Vantor Insider's weekly countdown shows the removal clock at its worst, with harbor tugs and switcher locomotives hammering at $40,000 landing at $98,000 because buyers get 10 business days before $50 per hour demurrage starts accruing [WGe7vjs5ktc @ 00:15:49]. Even soft goods carry a condition tax. Gear Rack sets aside an unacceptable-condition 2XL pair of APFU shorts rather than ship it, inventory that never goes out the door on a truckload buy [m4wTDvPYQuA @ 00:16:29]. Across every lot, the cheap number hides a second invoice, and the operator who prices that invoice before bidding is the only one who profits.

callout.title: Stop-Bid Checks Before the Paddle Goes Up
callout.body: Every item below is a loss the practitioners watched buyers take after winning. Clear all four on the listing and data plate before committing a dollar.
items: Do not bid on any MEP unit until the data plate middle digit reads zero for 60 Hz output and the analog hour counter matches the preservation tag [Vantor Surplus — VA8oRw7jQuQ @ 00:20:09].
Do not bid on any tactical truck until the lot confirms its demilitarization code and an original standard form 97 issued at the time of sale [Vantor Insider — vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:03:00].
Do not bid on a $25 to $100 transformer, communication shelter or skid chiller until the environmental rider on PCBs and asbestos is read [Vantor Insider — vkoGZ6Y4EhU @ 00:15:04].
Do not bid until trailer and pickup are lined up inside the 10 working day removal window, because daily storage penalties erase the savings [Vantor Surplus — VKFtBFmCW4U @ 00:04:13].

chapters.question_prompt: What do school district, university, and municipal surplus sales offer, and how do resellers flip those lots for profit?
chapters.title: Local Surplus Sales and Flipping the Lots
chapters.subtitle: School district, university, city, and state surplus auction days, GovDeals flips with real numbers and custom software, GovDeals and liquidation freight math, eBay consignment, and reselling auction pallets on Whatnot
chapters.executive_summary: School districts, cities, police departments, state agencies and universities sell surplus on a regular schedule. They use GovDeals, live auctioneers and preview-day sales, and starting prices run from $5 to $100. Hammer prices often land far below original cost: iMacs at $100, a 3D printer at $500, a Tesla Model 3 near $6,000. The operators agree on the rules. Know your exit price before you bid. Inspect in person. Buy within pickup range. Skip low-margin categories. The working numbers are concrete: zero-turn mowers bought at $2,000 to $3,000 and flipped for $4,000 to $5,000, a 20 to 25 percent all-in cost target, and a 3-item cap on new GovDeals accounts. Results split hard. 2plot ai cleared about $1,500 after four months and called the model not sustainable. Resale Rabbit and Liquidation Motivation report $75 and $200 pallets turning into four-figure returns.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Local government surplus is a recurring pipeline, and every source here describes the same supply. At Bibb County Schools, inventory specialist Mike Fordham walks the warehouses, inventories what is there, and starts items at $100. Lots run “in to the thousands” online. The district plans sales “every three to six months,” and buyers range from farmers and community centers to foreign schools buying buses [QOcs7dzmhGk @ 00:00:35]. In Springfield, Florida Auction Network sold Crown Victorias, Harley-Davidsons and work trucks pulled from Panama City PD, Public Works, Panama City Beach PD and the Bay County Sheriff's Office. 102 of 149 items sold, mostly to repeat buyers. One first-timer came to “make investments in turn around and make a little extra cash” [5kDb2ezDhgo @ 00:01:02]. Sacramento's state surplus sale draws from state agencies, CHP confiscations and TSA surrenders, with prices from “$5” to “thousands” [9u351Sc6VXo @ 00:02:42]. At the OSU Technical College annual sale, Adam of R25 Country watched about 40 iMacs go as one lot for $775. A 3D printer that cost “40 something,000” new sold for $500, while other items “they couldn't give away” [sbKbkYznbo4 @ 00:20:47]. The crowd that shows up sets the floor. Flippers make their money on the gap between original cost and hammer price.

Before any money moves, every reseller follows the same rule: know the exit price. Shannon Jean puts it flatly: “I always tell you don't buy anything unless you know what you can sell it for.” She adds “Don't buy a vehicle without inspecting it,” and tells buyers to question sellers and schedule inspections on anything they can't verify from photos [u0nFlfog1Y0 @ 00:11:46]. At the City of Jackson impound sale of more than 500 seized, abandoned and stolen vehicles, organizers say some vehicles don't run. They say “We don't guarantee title, but we gonna give you the paperwork you need to get a title,” and tell first-timers to “bring somebody with you” [rAJhvok5Ewk @ 00:00:12]. Chase Thrifts learned the floor-level version at the IUPUI surplus auction. Arrive early: working and non-working tags can't be read from 30 feet away, and once the crowd fills in you are bidding blind on electronics [aKiF3bLLJJ4 @ 00:01:52]. Sacramento's state sale builds this in with a full preview window from 9:00 to 3:00 the day before the 10:00 auction. Lines get long, so the preview is where serious buyers do their sorting [9u351Sc6VXo @ 00:01:46]. The consensus: inspect first, price second, bid last. Inspection is what separates a $10 win from a dead lot you still have to haul.

The third point of agreement: margin and logistics decide whether a lot is a deal, not the hammer price. 2plot ai avoids low-margin categories like clothes and looks for items that are expensive to buy into but carry high margin. The account also warns that new GovDeals accounts can win only 3 items, and that failing to pick up gets you banned [R8bNgZVNLAk @ 00:02:40]. Shannon Jean stresses that GovDeals requires pickup, unlike shipped B-Stock lots. Buy close or send the job through uShip, and lock in pickup dates with the seller right after winning [u0nFlfog1Y0 @ 00:06:04]. Competition is the other filter. At IUPUI, repair companies were “buying out everything” and computers sold by the pallet for thousands. Chase Thrifts came away with a single $10 lot, a sign of how hard the crowded categories are for small buyers [aKiF3bLLJJ4 @ 00:01:18]. Side Stacks answers with geography: rural areas have less competition, and the play “really just depends on where you live and what is for sale in your area.” Operators should also use their own skills to fix, repaint or repurpose what other buyers pass on [JwkoiixPFmM @ 00:09:20]. The operator who controls transport, picks categories with room in them and avoids crowded lanes keeps the spread.
